rubric.point: Formation of energy bands from overlap of atomic orbitals (definition of valence band, conduction band, forbidden gap E<sub>g</sub>)
Conductor: overlapping bands / partly filled band, E<sub>g</sub> = 0, with labelled band diagram
Insulator: completely filled VB, empty CB, large gap (E<sub>g</sub> > 5 eV), with labelled band diagram
Semiconductor: small gap (≈ 0.7–1.1 eV), conductivity rises with temperature, with labelled band diagram
Tabular comparison (E<sub>g</sub>, resistivity, temperature effect, examples)

answer: Band theory (MO theory applied to solids): in a solid containing N atoms, the N atomic orbitals of each energy level overlap to give N closely spaced molecular orbitals. Because N ≈ 1023, the spacing is so small that the levels merge into a continuous energy band.

Valence band (VB): the highest energy band filled with valence electrons (at 0 K). Conduction band (CB): the next higher band, empty or partly filled, whose electrons are free to move and carry current. Forbidden gap (Eg): the energy region between the top of the VB and the bottom of the CB in which no electron state exists.

1. Conductors (metals): either the VB is only partly filled or the VB and CB overlap, so Eg = 0. A very small electric field can move electrons to vacant levels immediately. Conductivity is high (107 S m-1) and decreases as temperature rises because lattice vibrations scatter electrons. Examples: Cu, Ag, Na, Al.

2. Insulators: the VB is completely filled, the CB is empty and Eg is large (> 5 eV, e.g. diamond ≈ 6 eV). Thermal or electrical energy available at ordinary temperature cannot lift electrons across the gap, so there is practically no conduction. Resistivity ≈ 1010–1020 Ω m. Examples: diamond, glass, mica, rubber.

3. Semiconductors: the VB is filled and the CB empty at 0 K (behaves like an insulator) but Eg is small (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV). At room temperature some electrons are excited to the CB, leaving holes in the VB; both carry current. Conductivity increases with temperature (and with doping: n-type, p-type).

Diagram to draw: three vertical energy axes side by side. (a) Conductor: VB and CB overlapping, no gap. (b) Insulator: shaded VB at bottom, empty CB at top, wide gap labelled Eg > 5 eV. (c) Semiconductor: shaded VB, empty CB, narrow gap labelled Eg ≈ 1 eV. Label VB, CB, Eg and the Fermi level.

Comparison: Conductor – Eg = 0, resistivity 10-8 Ω m, resistance increases with T, free electrons are many. Semiconductor – Eg ≈ 1 eV, resistivity 10-4–104 Ω m, resistance decreases with T. Insulator – Eg > 5 eV, resistivity > 1010 Ω m, essentially no carriers.
Conclusion: the width of the forbidden gap, and the filling of the bands, decides whether a solid is a conductor, semiconductor or insulator.

rubric.point: MO energy-level diagram of CO (14 e⁻) with correct ordering, labelled AOs and MOs
CO electronic configuration and bond order = 3
MO energy-level diagram of NO (15 e⁻) with electron filling
NO electronic configuration and bond order = 2.5
Magnetic behaviour of CO (diamagnetic) and NO (paramagnetic) with reason
Reference to 2s–2p mixing / use of MO ordering (π2p below σ2p)

answer: Basis: CO and NO are heteronuclear diatomic molecules with 14 and 15 electrons; like N2 (2s–2p mixing present) the order of MOs is σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < π2px = π2py < σ2pz < π*2px = π*2py < σ*2pz (2s–2p mixing). The more electronegative atom (O) has its AOs at lower energy, so bonding MOs are closer to O and antibonding MOs closer to C (or N).

Diagram of CO: on the left put the AOs of C (1s, 2s, 2p), on the right those of O (lower in energy); in the centre draw the MOs in the above order, joined to the parent AOs by dashed lines. Fill the 14 electrons with arrows by the Aufbau principle, Pauli principle and Hund's rule.
Configuration of CO (6 + 8 = 14 e⁻): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2px² π2py² σ2pz². (The 1s pair is non-bonding core in practice.)
Bond order of CO: Nb = 10, Na = 4, so B.O. = (Nb − Na)/2 = (10 − 4)/2 = 3 (triple bond C≡O, isoelectronic with N2).
Magnetism of CO: all 14 electrons are paired in the MOs (no electron in π*), hence CO is diamagnetic.
Configuration of NO (7 + 8 = 15 e⁻): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2px² π2py² σ2pz² π*2px¹ (π*2py⁰). The 15th electron enters one of the degenerate π* orbitals.
Bond order of NO: Nb = 10, Na = 5, so B.O. = (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5.
Magnetism of NO: one unpaired electron in π*2p, so NO is paramagnetic (μ = √[n(n+2)] = √3 = 1.73 BM).

Why CO is diamagnetic but NO is paramagnetic: CO has an even number of electrons (14) which exactly fill the bonding MOs, leaving π* empty, so every spin is paired. NO has an odd number (15); the extra electron must go in the antibonding π*2p orbital and cannot be paired. Removing it gives NO+ (B.O. 3, diamagnetic) – hence NO is easily ionised and its bond is stronger in NO+.
Q1.2.diagram: Two MO diagrams (CO and NO): AOs of the two atoms on the sides (O lower than C or N), MOs in the centre in the order σ2s, σ*2s, π2p (x,y), σ2p<sub>z</sub>, π*2p (x,y), σ*2p<sub>z</sub>, with electrons as arrows; show the single electron in π* for NO.

rubric.point: Labelled MO energy-level diagram of O<sub>2</sub> (σ2p<sub>z</sub> lies below π2p for O<sub>2</sub>)
Electronic configuration of O<sub>2</sub> (16 e⁻)
Bond order of O<sub>2</sub> = 2
Explanation of paramagnetism (two unpaired electrons in π*2p, Hund's rule)
B.O. and magnetic nature of O<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, O<sub>2</sub><sup>-</sup>, O<sub>2</sub><sup>2-</sup> (0.75 each)
Correct order of bond length / stability

answer: MO theory for O2: two oxygen atoms (1s² 2s² 2p⁴) combine through LCAO; 16 electrons in total. For O2 and heavier diatomics the 2s–2p mixing is negligible, so the energy order is: σ1s < σ*1s < σ2s < σ*2s < σ2pz < π2px = π2py < π*2px = π*2py < σ*2pz.

Diagram: AOs of oxygen atom A (left) and B (right); the MOs in the centre in the above order; 16 electrons filled with arrows (Aufbau, Pauli, Hund). The two electrons of the π* pair are drawn as ↑ in π*2px and ↑ in π*2py.
Electronic configuration of O2: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² σ2pz² π2px² π2py² π*2px¹ π*2py¹.
Bond order: Nb = 10, Na = 6; B.O. = (10 − 6)/2 = 2 (O=O double bond).

Paramagnetism: by Hund's rule the last two electrons occupy the two degenerate π*2p orbitals singly with parallel spins. Two unpaired electrons give a net magnetic moment μ = √[n(n+2)] = √8 = 2.83 BM, so liquid O2 is attracted by a magnet. (Lewis/VB theory fails to explain this – a major success of MOT.)
O2+ (15 e⁻): one electron removed from π*: ... π*2px¹. B.O. = (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5; one unpaired electron – paramagnetic.
O2- (superoxide, 17 e⁻): ... π*2px² π*2py¹. B.O. = (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5; one unpaired electron – paramagnetic.
O22- (peroxide, 18 e⁻): ... π*2px² π*2py². B.O. = (10 − 8)/2 = 1; no unpaired electron – diamagnetic.
Summary / trend: Bond order: O2+ (2.5) > O2 (2) > O2- (1.5) > O22- (1). Bond length and stability follow the order: bond length O22- > O2- > O2 > O2+; bond energy is in the reverse order.

rubric.point: Electronic configurations of CO (14 e⁻) and CO<sup>+</sup> (13 e⁻)
Bond order of CO = 3 and of CO<sup>+</sup> = 2.5
Relation: higher bond order → shorter bond length / greater bond energy
Conclusion: CO shorter than CO<sup>+</sup>; (CO<sup>+</sup> paramagnetic)

answer: Configuration of CO (14 e⁻): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2px² π2py² σ2pz². Bonding electrons Nb = 10, antibonding Na = 4.
Bond order of CO: (10 − 4)/2 = 3 (C≡O triple bond).
Configuration of CO+ (13 e⁻): the electron is removed from the highest filled MO, σ2pz, which is a bonding orbital: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2px² π2py² σ2pz¹. So Nb = 9, Na = 4.
Bond order of CO+: (9 − 4)/2 = 2.5.

Relation: bond length is inversely related to bond order, and bond dissociation energy is directly related to it. Greater bond order means more electron density between the nuclei, a stronger pull on both nuclei, and a shorter bond.
Conclusion: since B.O.(CO) = 3 > B.O.(CO+) = 2.5, CO has the shorter and stronger bond than CO+ (also CO is diamagnetic, CO+ paramagnetic with one unpaired electron).

rubric.point: Definition and postulates of CFT (point charges, electrostatic repulsion, no orbital overlap, ligand field)
Five d-orbitals and why they split (e<sub>g</sub> pointing at ligands, t<sub>2g</sub> between them)
Octahedral splitting: e<sub>g</sub> up (+0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>), t<sub>2g</sub> down (−0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>), with labelled diagram
Tetrahedral splitting: e down (−0.6Δ<sub>t</sub>), t<sub>2</sub> up (+0.4Δ<sub>t</sub>), with labelled diagram
Δ<sub>t</sub> = (4/9)Δ<sub>o</sub>, tetrahedral complexes high spin; strong/weak field and pairing energy

answer: Definition: Crystal Field Theory (Bethe, Van Vleck) explains the bonding, colour and magnetism of transition-metal complexes by considering the metal–ligand interaction as purely electrostatic, and studies how the ligand field removes the degeneracy of the five d-orbitals of the central metal ion.

Postulates: (1) The ligands are treated as point negative charges (or dipoles) and the metal ion as a positive charge. (2) The bond between metal and ligand is purely ionic; there is no orbital overlap. (3) In the free ion the five d-orbitals are degenerate; in the field of the ligands they repel the ligand charges and the degeneracy is lost. (4) The d-orbitals that point towards the ligands are raised more in energy than those that point between them. (5) The splitting depends on the nature of the ligand, the geometry and the metal ion; whether electrons pair or not depends on splitting energy Δ versus pairing energy P.
The d-orbitals: dxy, dyz, dzx have lobes between the axes (t2g set); dx²−y² and dz² have lobes along the axes (eg set).

Octahedral field (Oh): six ligands approach along ±x, ±y, ±z. The eg orbitals point directly at the ligands, so they experience strong repulsion and rise in energy; the t2g orbitals avoid the ligands and are relatively lower. The gap is Δo (10 Dq). By the barycentre rule: t2g lies 0.4Δo (−4 Dq) below and eg lies 0.6Δo (+6 Dq) above the average (hypothetical spherical-field) level.

Diagram (octahedral): draw the bare-ion level at the centre, raised spherical-field level, and on the right the eg (dx²−y², dz²) at +0.6Δo and t2g (dxy, dyz, dzx) at −0.4Δo, with Δo marked between them.

Tetrahedral field (Td): four ligands occupy alternate corners of a cube. Now the lobes of dxy, dyz, dzx (t2) lie closer to the ligands, whereas dx²−y², dz² (e) point to the face centres, away from the ligands. Hence the order is reversed: t2 is raised by +0.4Δt and e lowered by −0.6Δt. (No ‘g’ subscript, as there is no centre of symmetry.)

Magnitude: with only four ligands and no direct pointing at the lobes, Δt = (4/9)Δo ≈ 0.44Δo for the same metal and ligand. Because Δt is almost always smaller than the pairing energy P, tetrahedral complexes are practically always high spin.

Spin states (octahedral, d⁴–d⁷): if Δo < P (weak-field ligands such as I-, Br-, Cl-, F-, H2O) electrons occupy eg before pairing – high spin. If Δo > P (strong-field ligands such as NH3, en, CN-, CO) electrons pair in t2g first – low spin. Spectrochemical series: I- < Br- < Cl- < F- < OH- < H2O < NH3 < en < NO2- < CN- < CO.
Success: CFT explains colour (d–d transitions of energy Δ), magnetism and the stability (CFSE) of complexes.
formulas: Spin state: Δ < P → high spin; Δ > P → low spin

rubric.point: Ni<sup>2+</sup> is d⁸ (3d⁸) and the oxidation state/electron count
[Ni(CN)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>: CN<sup>-</sup> strong-field ligand, large splitting, d<sub>x²−y²</sub> very high, electrons pair, dsp² square planar
Electron filling → no unpaired electrons → diamagnetic (μ = 0)
[NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>: Cl<sup>-</sup> weak-field ligand, small Δ<sub>t</sub> (4/9 Δ<sub>o</sub>), tetrahedral sp³, splitting diagram
e⁴t₂⁴ configuration, 2 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic, μ = 2.83 BM; comparison

answer: Metal ion: in both complexes nickel is Ni2+: Ni (3d⁸ 4s²) → Ni2+ = [Ar] 3d⁸. The geometry (and hence magnetism) is decided by the strength of the ligand field.

[Ni(CN)4]2-: CN- is a strong-field ligand (π-acceptor, high in the spectrochemical series). It produces a very large crystal field splitting, so the eight d-electrons prefer to pair up. In a square planar field (ligands along ±x, ±y) the dx²−y² orbital, pointing directly at the four ligands, is raised very high in energy, and the other four orbitals (dxy, dz², dxz, dyz) are lower.

Electron filling: the eight electrons of Ni2+ fill the four lower orbitals in pairs (dxz² dyz² dz²² dxy²) leaving the high-energy dx²−y² empty. The energy gap to dx²−y² is greater than the pairing energy, so no electron is promoted. This gives dsp² hybridisation (one 3d, 4s, two 4p orbitals) and a square planar shape.
Magnetism: all electrons are paired, so n = 0 and μ = √[n(n+2)] = 0; [Ni(CN)4]2- is diamagnetic.

[NiCl4]2-: Cl- is a weak-field ligand. The four ligands arrange themselves tetrahedrally (minimum ligand–ligand repulsion), where the splitting Δt = (4/9)Δo is so small that it cannot overcome the pairing energy. The d-orbitals split into a lower e set (dz², dx²−y²) and an upper t2 set (dxy, dyz, dzx).

Electron filling: 8 electrons: e⁴ (all four paired in the lower set) and t2⁴ (two paired in one orbital, two unpaired in the other two orbitals by Hund's rule). The configuration is e⁴ t2⁴ with sp³ hybridisation.
Magnetism: two unpaired electrons, so [NiCl4]2- is paramagnetic with μ = √(2×4) = √8 = 2.83 BM.
Comparison: square planar [Ni(CN)4]2-: strong field, dsp², low spin, 0 unpaired e⁻, diamagnetic. Tetrahedral [NiCl4]2-: weak field, sp³, high spin, 2 unpaired e⁻, paramagnetic.

Conclusion: the difference arises purely from the position of CN- and Cl- in the spectrochemical series: a strong-field ligand forces pairing and square planar d⁸ geometry; a weak-field ligand gives tetrahedral geometry with unpaired electrons.
formulas: [NiCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>: sp³, tetrahedral, e⁴t<sub>2</sub>⁴, n = 2, μ = 2.83 BM

rubric.point: Electronic configuration of Co<sup>3+</sup> (3d⁶) and oxidation-state working
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>: strong-field NH<sub>3</sub> causes pairing, vacating two 3d orbitals; d²sp³ orbital diagram
Inner-orbital (low-spin) character, octahedral, no unpaired electrons, diamagnetic (μ = 0)
Electronic configuration of Ni<sup>2+</sup> (3d⁸)
[Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>: sp³d² with 4s, 4p, 4d orbitals (outer orbital), two unpaired 3d electrons, μ = 2.83 BM, paramagnetic; reason for not forming d²sp³
Supporting CFT explanation (t<sub>2g</sub>⁶ for Co<sup>3+</sup>; t<sub>2g</sub>⁶e<sub>g</sub>² for Ni<sup>2+</sup>)

answer: Valence bond approach: the ligand donates a lone pair into a vacant hybrid orbital of the metal ion. If the hybrid uses the inner (n−1)d orbitals the complex is inner orbital (low spin); if it uses the outer nd orbitals it is outer orbital (high spin).
[Co(NH3)6]3+: oxidation state of Co: x + 6(0) = +3, so Co3+. Co: [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s², Co3+: [Ar] 3d⁶ (4 unpaired electrons in the free ion).

NH3 is a strong-field ligand: the six 3d electrons are forced to pair up in three orbitals (↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓), leaving two 3d orbitals vacant. These two 3d, the 4s and three 4p orbitals mix to give six equivalent d²sp³ hybrid orbitals directed to the corners of an octahedron; each accepts a lone pair from one NH3.
Because the inner 3d orbitals are used, it is an inner orbital (low spin) complex. There is no unpaired electron (n = 0, μ = 0), so the complex is diamagnetic.
CFT view: Δo (strong field NH3) > P, so Co3+ has the configuration t2g⁶ eg⁰ – fully paired.

[Ni(NH3)6]2+: Ni2+ has configuration [Ar] 3d⁸ (Ni: 3d⁸ 4s²; 2 electrons from 4s removed). Eight electrons in five d-orbitals: even after maximum pairing (↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑↓ and one empty) only one 3d orbital could be emptied, but two empty d-orbitals are needed for d²sp³.

Hence Ni2+ cannot use inner 3d orbitals; the two unpaired 3d electrons remain, and the metal uses one 4s, three 4p and two 4d orbitals to form sp³d² hybrids (octahedral). This is an outer orbital (high spin) complex.
Two unpaired electrons: μ = √[n(n+2)] = √8 = 2.83 BM, so the complex is paramagnetic.
CFT view: an octahedral d⁸ ion always has the configuration t2g⁶ eg², i.e. two unpaired electrons in eg, irrespective of the field strength, so it is always paramagnetic.
Conclusion: Co3+(d⁶) with strong-field NH3 – d²sp³, inner orbital, diamagnetic; Ni2+(d⁸) – sp³d², outer orbital, paramagnetic.

rubric.point: Main postulates of VBT (any 4, 0.5 each)
Limitations of VBT (any 3)
XeF<sub>4</sub>: sp³d² hybridisation, square planar, 2 lone pairs
XeO<sub>4</sub>: sp³ hybridisation, tetrahedral, with dπ–pπ bonding

answer: Postulates of VBT (Heitler–London, Pauling): (1) A covalent bond forms by the overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals of two atoms having electrons of opposite spin; the pair is shared. (2) The greater the overlap, the stronger the bond; bonds form in the direction of maximum overlap. (3) A σ bond is formed by head-on overlap, and a π bond by lateral overlap. (4) The number of bonds equals the number of unpaired electrons (valency); atoms can be promoted to get more unpaired electrons. (5) Atomic orbitals of comparable energy hybridise to give equivalent hybrid orbitals of definite geometry.

Limitations: (1) It cannot explain the paramagnetism of O2 (predicts all electrons paired). (2) It treats electrons as localised and does not explain delocalised bonding, e.g. in benzene (needs resonance). (3) It does not explain the existence of odd-electron species such as H2+, and the colour/spectra of complexes. (4) It does not give energies of excited states; no quantitative information about bond energies for polyatomic molecules.

XeF4: Xe (5s² 5p⁶) – two electrons are promoted from 5p to 5d giving four unpaired electrons which bond to four F atoms. Hybridisation: sp³d² (octahedral arrangement of 6 electron pairs: 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs, placed trans to each other). Structure: square planar, F–Xe–F = 90°.
XeO4: Xe is promoted to its 8-electron (4 unpaired) state (5s¹ 5p³ 5d⁴); four σ bonds with O using sp³ hybrids, and four π (pπ–dπ) bonds. Structure: tetrahedral, O–Xe–O = 109.5°, no lone pair.

rubric.point: Hybridisation concept (definition, mixing of orbitals) – introduction
H<sub>2</sub>O: sp³ hybridisation, 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs, bent shape, ~104.5°, with figure
NH<sub>3</sub>: sp³ hybridisation, 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair, trigonal pyramidal, ~107°, with figure
SF<sub>6</sub>: sp³d² hybridisation, octahedral, 90°, with figure and promotion of electrons

answer: Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of the same atom with nearly equal energies to give an equal number of equivalent hybrid orbitals with definite orientation. The geometry (arrangement of electron pairs) follows the type of hybridisation, whereas the shape (arrangement of atoms) additionally depends on lone pairs.

H2O: central O (2s² 2p⁴) forms two σ bonds with H using two sp³ hybrid orbitals; the other two sp³ orbitals hold lone pairs. Steric number = 4 → sp³, tetrahedral electron geometry. Because lone pair–lone pair repulsion > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, the H–O–H angle is compressed from 109.5° to 104.5°. Molecular shape: bent (V-shaped).

NH3: N (2s² 2p³) has three half-filled 2p orbitals; one 2s and three 2p mix to give four sp³ hybrid orbitals. Three form σ bonds with H 1s, the fourth holds the lone pair. Steric number = 4 → sp³ (tetrahedral geometry). The lone pair repels the bond pairs more and compresses H–N–H to 107°. Shape: trigonal pyramidal.

SF6: ground-state S (3s² 3p⁴) has only two unpaired electrons. For six bonds, one 3s and one 3p electron are promoted to vacant 3d orbitals, giving six unpaired electrons (3s¹ 3p³ 3d²). One 3s, three 3p and two 3d orbitals mix to give six equivalent sp³d² hybrid orbitals pointing to the corners of a regular octahedron; each overlaps with a 2p orbital of F. All six S–F bonds are equal and F–S–F angle is 90°. Geometry and shape: octahedral (no lone pair, non-polar, μ = 0).
Summary table: H2O – sp³, 2 bp + 2 lp, bent, 104.5°; NH3 – sp³, 3 bp + 1 lp, pyramidal, 107°; SF6 – sp³d², 6 bp + 0 lp, octahedral, 90°.

rubric.point: Physical significance of ψ (amplitude, no direct physical meaning, may be complex, probability amplitude)
Significance of ψ² (or ψψ*): probability density, normalisation ∫ψ²dτ = 1
de Broglie hypothesis λ = h/mv and its significance (wave nature, Davisson–Germer, Bohr condition)
Heisenberg uncertainty principle Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π and its significance (definite orbits replaced by probability orbitals)
Concluding remark linking these to the wave-mechanical atom

answer: Wave function (ψ): in quantum mechanics the state of an electron is described by a mathematical function ψ(x, y, z) obtained by solving the Schrödinger wave equation. ψ is the amplitude of the electron wave. It has no direct physical meaning (it can be negative or complex and is not measurable), but it contains all the information about the system; it is called the probability amplitude. For a given orbital the sign of ψ gives the phase of the wave (+ve/−ve lobes), which is important for bonding.

Significance of ψ²: the square of the amplitude (for complex ψ, |ψ|² = ψψ*) gives the probability density, i.e. the probability of finding the electron per unit volume at the point (x, y, z). The probability of finding the electron in a small volume dτ is ψ²dτ.

Normalisation: since the electron must be somewhere in space, ∫ψ² dτ over all space = 1. A wave function satisfying this is normalised. The orbital (region of high ψ²) is the space around the nucleus where the probability of finding the electron is about 90–95%. For ψ to be acceptable it must be single-valued, finite and continuous.
de Broglie hypothesis: every moving particle has a wave associated with it, with wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv (h = 6.626×10-34 J s). For an electron accelerated through V volts, λ = 12.27/√V Å.

Significance of de Broglie hypothesis: (i) It explains the stability of Bohr orbits: a standing wave exists only when the circumference of the orbit is a whole number of wavelengths, 2πr = nλ, giving mvr = nh/2π (quantisation of angular momentum). (ii) It was verified by the Davisson–Germer electron diffraction experiment and G. P. Thomson's experiment; this is the basis of the electron microscope and electron diffraction. (iii) It laid the foundation of wave mechanics (Schrödinger). (iv) The wavelength is measurable only for microscopic particles; for a cricket ball λ ≈ 10-34 m is undetectable.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: it is impossible to determine simultaneously both the exact position and exact momentum of a microscopic particle: Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π (or ΔE · Δt ≥ h/4π).

Significance of the uncertainty principle: (i) The concept of definite orbits (Bohr) is untenable; only the probability of finding the electron (orbitals) can be given. (ii) It explains why an electron cannot exist inside the nucleus (confinement to Δx ≈ 10-15 m would require a kinetic energy far larger than nuclear binding energy). (iii) It is negligible for macroscopic bodies (e.g. a 1 mg particle) but important for electrons. (iv) It follows from the wave nature of matter and justifies the use of ψ² as probability.

Conclusion: ψ and ψ² describe the electron statistically; de Broglie's relation gives the wave character and Heisenberg's principle sets the limit of precision, together leading to the modern quantum-mechanical model.

rubric.point: Starting classical wave equation for a wave in 3D
Separation ψ(x,y,z)e<sup>−iωt</sup> and reduction to ∇²ψ + (4π²/λ²)ψ = 0
Use of de Broglie relation λ = h/mv
Kinetic energy ½mv² = E − V substituted
Final equation ∇²ψ + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0 (3D)
Hamiltonian form Ĥψ = Eψ and conditions on ψ

answer: Postulate: a moving particle has a wave associated with it (de Broglie). Schrödinger (1926) treated the matter wave like a classical standing wave and obtained a differential equation for it.
Step 1 – classical wave equation: for a wave of velocity u and amplitude Ψ(x, y, z, t): ∂²Ψ/∂x² + ∂²Ψ/∂y² + ∂²Ψ/∂z² = (1/u²) ∂²Ψ/∂t², i.e. ∇²Ψ = (1/u²)∂²Ψ/∂t².
Step 2 – separate the variables: for a stationary state, Ψ(x, y, z, t) = ψ(x, y, z) e−iωt, where ψ depends only on position. Then ∂²Ψ/∂t² = −ω² ψ e−iωt, so ∇²ψ = −(ω²/u²) ψ, i.e. ∇²ψ + (ω²/u²)ψ = 0.
Step 3 – use ω = 2πν and u = νλ: ω/u = 2πν/νλ = 2π/λ. Hence ∇²ψ + (4π²/λ²) ψ = 0 … (1).
Step 4 – de Broglie relation: λ = h/mv, so 1/λ² = m²v²/h². Substituting in (1): ∇²ψ + (4π²m²v²/h²) ψ = 0 … (2).
Step 5 – energy relation: total energy E = kinetic + potential = ½mv² + V, so ½mv² = E − V, i.e. m²v² = 2m(E − V) … (3).
Step 6 – substitute (3) in (2): ∇²ψ + (4π²/h²) · 2m(E − V) ψ = 0.
Result – time-independent Schrödinger equation in 3D: ∇²ψ + (8π²m/h²)(E − V)ψ = 0, where ∇² = ∂²/∂x² + ∂²/∂y² + ∂²/∂z².
Hamiltonian form: rearranging, −(h²/8π²m)∇²ψ + Vψ = Eψ, i.e. Ĥψ = Eψ, with Ĥ = −(ħ²/2m)∇² + V (ħ = h/2π) the Hamiltonian operator and E the eigenvalue (energy).

Conditions on ψ: acceptable solutions must be single-valued, finite and continuous, with continuous first derivative, and normalisable (∫ψ²dτ = 1); only for certain values of E (eigenvalues) are such solutions possible – this gives quantisation of energy.
Special case: for a free particle V = 0, ∇²ψ + (8π²mE/h²)ψ = 0.

answer: Given: m = 9.1 × 10-31 kg, v = 40 m s-1, uncertainty in momentum = 10-6 (taken as the fraction 10-6 of the momentum), h = 6.626 × 10-34 J s. To find: Δx.

Momentum: p = mv = 9.1 × 10-31 × 40 = 3.64 × 10-29 kg m s-1.
Uncertainty in momentum: Δp = 10-6 × p = 10-6 × 3.64 × 10-29 = 3.64 × 10-35 kg m s-1.

rubric.point: Statement of Nernst equation and definition of ΔG, Q, E°
Derivation of the cell form: ΔG = −nFE and ΔG° = −nFE° substituted in ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q
Final cell equation E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q and its 298 K form E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q
Derivation of single electrode potential E = E° + (0.0591/n) log[M<sup>n+</sup>] for M<sup>n+</sup> + ne<sup>−</sup> → M
Engineering applications (any three: pH, corrosion tendency, concentration cells, solubility product, equilibrium constant, potentiometric titration)

answer: Nernst equation relates the electrode/cell potential to the standard potential and the activities (concentrations) of the species taking part in the redox change at temperature T.
Step 1 – Free energy of a general reaction. For aA + bB → cC + dD at constant T and P, the van't Hoff isotherm gives ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q = [C]c[D]d / ([A]a[B]b) is the reaction quotient.

Step 2 – Link with electrical work. The maximum useful (electrical) work obtained from a cell equals the decrease in free energy: −ΔG = nFE, so ΔG = −nFE. Under standard conditions ΔG° = −nFE° (F = 96500 C mol−1, n = electrons transferred).
Step 3 – Substitution. −nFE = −nFE° + RT ln Q. Dividing by −nF:
E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q … (cell Nernst equation).
Step 4 – Numerical form. At 298 K, R = 8.314 J K−1 mol−1, F = 96500 C: 2.303RT/F = 0.0591 V. Hence E = E° − (0.0591/n) log10 Q.
Single electrode potential. For the reduction half-reaction Mn+ + ne− → M(s), Q = aM/aMn+ = 1/[Mn+] (activity of pure solid = 1). Applying the same derivation:
EMn+/M = E° − (RT/nF) ln (1/[Mn+]) = E° + (0.0591/n) log[Mn+] at 298 K.
Cell example (Daniell cell). Zn + Cu2+ → Zn2+ + Cu; Q = [Zn2+]/[Cu2+], so Ecell = E°cell − (0.0591/2) log([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]).

Engineering applications: (i) calculation of pH with hydrogen/glass electrodes, E = E° − 0.0591 pH; (ii) predicting corrosion tendency and feasibility of a redox reaction under non-standard conditions; (iii) concentration cells and ion-selective electrodes; (iv) determination of equilibrium constant (at equilibrium E = 0, log K = nE°/0.0591) and solubility product of sparingly soluble salts; (v) potentiometric titrations and battery voltage estimation.

rubric.point: Neat labelled diagram of Daniell cell (electrodes, electrolytes, salt bridge, voltmeter, direction of e<sup>−</sup> and ion flow)

answer: Galvanic (voltaic) cell: a device that converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. The Daniell cell is the standard example.

Construction: A zinc rod dipped in 1 M ZnSO4 solution forms the anode half-cell; a copper rod dipped in 1 M CuSO4 solution forms the cathode half-cell. The two solutions are connected internally by a salt bridge (U-tube containing agar–agar gel saturated with KCl or KNO3) and externally by a metallic wire through a voltmeter/load.

Function of salt bridge: completes the internal circuit, maintains electrical neutrality of both half-cells by migration of ions, and eliminates the liquid-junction potential. K+ and Cl− are chosen because their ionic mobilities are almost equal.
Anode (oxidation, negative): Zn(s) → Zn2+(aq) + 2e−.
Cathode (reduction, positive): Cu2+(aq) + 2e− → Cu(s).
Overall cell reaction: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s).
Cell representation: Zn(s) | Zn2+(C1) ∥ Cu2+(C2) | Cu(s), anode on the left, cathode on the right, ∥ = salt bridge.
Flow: electrons flow from Zn to Cu through the external wire, conventional current from Cu to Zn; anions move towards the anode and cations towards the cathode through the salt bridge.
EMF: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (both as reduction potentials) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
Nernst form: Ecell = E°cell − (0.0591/2) log([Zn2+]/[Cu2+]) at 298 K.

rubric.point: First law: statement and mathematical form ΔU = q − w (or q + w) with sign convention
Explanation: internal energy, work, heat, ΔH = ΔU + PΔn<sub>g</sub>RT, an example
Second law: any two standard statements (Kelvin–Planck / Clausius / entropy form)
Explanation of spontaneity, ΔS<sub>universe</sub> > 0, Carnot efficiency or ΔS = q<sub>rev</sub>/T
Applications / limitations or comparison of the two laws

answer: Thermodynamic system: the part of the universe under study; the rest is the surroundings. State functions (U, H, S, G) depend only on initial and final states.
First law (law of conservation of energy): Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. Equivalently, the energy of an isolated system is constant.

Mathematical form: ΔU = q − w, where q = heat absorbed by the system, w = work done by the system (w = PΔV for expansion). For an infinitesimal change dU = δq − δw. U is a state function; q and w are path functions.

Consequences: (a) at constant volume qv = ΔU; (b) at constant pressure qp = ΔH = ΔU + PΔV, so ΔH = ΔU + ΔngRT; (c) for an isothermal process of an ideal gas ΔU = 0 and q = w; (d) for an adiabatic process q = 0 and ΔU = −w. Hess's law is a direct result of the first law.
Limitation of the first law: it gives the energy balance but does not say in which direction a process will occur, nor why heat cannot be fully converted into work.
Second law – Kelvin–Planck statement: It is impossible to construct a cyclic engine which absorbs heat from a single reservoir and converts it completely into work without any other effect.
Clausius statement: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body without external work.

Entropy statement: For any spontaneous (irreversible) process the entropy of the universe increases: ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurr > 0; for a reversible process ΔStotal = 0. Entropy change is defined by dS = δqrev/T.

Explanation: Natural processes proceed towards greater disorder (e.g. gas expansion into vacuum, heat flow from hot to cold, mixing). The efficiency of any heat engine working between T1 (source) and T2 (sink) is η = (T1 − T2)/T1 < 1, so complete conversion of heat to work is impossible.
Applications: the second law gives the criterion of spontaneity (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0), efficiency of engines and refrigerators, and equilibrium conditions (ΔG = 0).

rubric.point: (i) Entropy: definition, dS = q<sub>rev</sub>/T, state function, units, physical meaning (disorder), entropy change criteria
(ii) Gibbs free energy: definition G = H − TS, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, criteria of spontaneity
(iii) Gibbs–Helmholtz equation statement/derivation
Applications of Gibbs–Helmholtz (ΔH from E and temperature coefficient, etc.)

answer: (i) Entropy (S): A thermodynamic state function that measures the randomness or disorder of a system. Defined by dS = δqrev/T; ΔS = qrev/T for an isothermal reversible change. Unit: J K−1 mol−1.

Physical meaning: S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid); entropy rises on melting, vaporisation, mixing and on increasing temperature. ΔS<sub>universe</sub> > 0 for spontaneous, = 0 for equilibrium (reversible) processes. For reactions ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants). Third law: S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K.
(ii) Gibbs free energy (G): G = H − TS, a state function that gives the maximum useful (non-expansion) work available from a system at constant T and P: −ΔG = wmax,useful.
At constant T and P: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Criteria: ΔG < 0 spontaneous (feasible); ΔG = 0 equilibrium; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous. Relations: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −nFE°.
(iii) Gibbs–Helmholtz equation: From G = H − TS and dG = V dP − S dT, at constant P: (∂G/∂T)P = −S. So G = H + T(∂G/∂T)P.
Hence ΔG = ΔH + T(∂ΔG/∂T)P, which on differentiating (ΔG/T) gives [∂(ΔG/T)/∂T]P = −ΔH/T².
For an electrochemical cell with ΔG = −nFE: −nFE = ΔH − nFT(∂E/∂T)P ⇒ ΔH = −nFE + nFT(∂E/∂T)P.

Applications: (a) finding ΔH of cell reactions from emf and temperature coefficient; (b) ΔS = nF(∂E/∂T)P; (c) effect of temperature on ΔG and on equilibrium constant (van't Hoff equation d ln K/dT = ΔH°/RT²); (d) predicting temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous, T = ΔH/ΔS.

rubric.point: Statement of Hess's law
Explanation with a worked example (e.g. C → CO<sub>2</sub> directly vs via CO), with energy-cycle diagram
Basis of the law (H is a state function)
Applications (at least four)
Limitations (at least two)

answer: Statement: The total enthalpy change of a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in several steps, provided the initial and final conditions (T, P, states of reactants and products) are the same. It depends only on initial and final states.
Basis: It is a direct consequence of the first law of thermodynamics and of enthalpy being a state function: ΔH is independent of the path.

Illustration: Formation of CO2 from carbon. Route 1 (direct): C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ. Route 2 (two steps): C(s) + ½O2 → CO(g), ΔH1 = −110.5 kJ; CO(g) + ½O2 → CO2(g), ΔH2 = −283.0 kJ. Sum: −110.5 − 283.0 = −393.5 kJ = ΔH. Hence ΔH = ΔH1 + ΔH2.
Energy cycle: draw C + O2 at the top, CO2 at the bottom, with a direct arrow (ΔH) and an indirect path through CO (ΔH1, ΔH2).

Applications: (a) enthalpy of formation of compounds that cannot be made directly, e.g. CO, CH4, C2H6 from heats of combustion; (b) enthalpy of transition between allotropes (graphite → diamond); (c) lattice energy through the Born–Haber cycle; (d) enthalpy of hydration and of neutralisation; (e) calculation of bond enthalpies; (f) calorific value of fuels.
Method: ΔH°reaction = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants) = ΣΔH°c(reactants) − ΣΔH°c(products).

Limitations: (a) applicable only when initial and final conditions (T, P, physical states, allotropic forms) are identical in all routes; (b) it gives only ΔH, not the rate or feasibility of the reaction; (c) data must be available for each step and ideal/consistent states are assumed; (d) it cannot be applied to reactions whose individual steps cannot be studied separately or whose enthalpy data are inaccurate; (e) enthalpy changes of dissolution depend on concentration.

rubric.point: Arrhenius concept: definition with examples and limitations
Brønsted–Lowry concept: proton donor/acceptor, conjugate pairs, examples, limitations
Lewis concept: electron-pair acceptor/donor, examples including coordinate bond formation
Comparison / relationship among the three theories

answer: 1. Arrhenius theory (1884): An acid is a substance that ionises in water to give H+ (H3O+) ions; a base ionises to give OH−. Examples: HCl → H+ + Cl−; NaOH → Na+ + OH−. Neutralisation: H+ + OH− → H2O.

Limitations: restricted to aqueous solutions; cannot explain basic nature of NH3 or Na2CO3 (no OH− in formula); cannot explain acid–base reactions in non-aqueous solvents or in gas phase (NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl).
2. Brønsted–Lowry theory (1923): An acid is a proton (H+) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Every acid has a conjugate base, and every base has a conjugate acid.

Examples: HCl + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup> (HCl acid, Cl<sup>−</sup> its conjugate base; H<sub>2</sub>O base, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> its conjugate acid); NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> (NH<sub>3</sub> base). Water is amphiprotic. A strong acid has a weak conjugate base.
Limitations: requires a transferable proton, so cannot explain acid behaviour of BF3, AlCl3, CO2, SO2.
3. Lewis theory (1923): An acid is a species that accepts an electron pair; a base is a species that donates an electron pair, forming a coordinate (dative) bond.

Examples: BF<sub>3</sub> + :NH<sub>3</sub> → F<sub>3</sub>B←NH<sub>3</sub> (BF<sub>3</sub> acid, NH<sub>3</sub> base); AlCl<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sup>−</sup> → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>; Ag<sup>+</sup> + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>; H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O; CO<sub>2</sub> + OH<sup>−</sup> → HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>. Lewis acids: electron-deficient molecules (BF<sub>3</sub>, AlCl<sub>3</sub>), cations (H<sup>+</sup>, Fe<sup>3+</sup>); Lewis bases: NH<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, Cl<sup>−</sup>, amines.

Comparison: Lewis ⊃ Brønsted–Lowry ⊃ Arrhenius in generality. Every Arrhenius acid/base is a Brønsted one, and every Brønsted acid/base is a Lewis one (H+ is the Lewis acid), but the reverse is not true. Lewis concept is most useful in organic catalysis and coordination chemistry.

rubric.point: Definition of Ellingham diagram: plot of ΔG° vs T for oxide formation per mole of O<sub>2</sub>, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°
Features: straight lines, slope = −ΔS°, kinks at phase changes, negative slope for most metals; C → CO line slopes down
Interpretation: lower line = more stable oxide; a metal reduces the oxide of any metal above it
Application to reducing agent selection (C, CO, Al, Mg) and temperature choice, e.g. smelting of ZnO / iron oxide

answer: Ellingham diagram is a graph of the standard free-energy change ΔG° for the formation of oxides (per mole of O2 consumed, 2M + O2 → 2MO) against temperature. It is based on ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, which has the form y = c + mx, so the plot is a straight line with slope −ΔS° and intercept ΔH°.

Features: (a) Since a gas (O2) is consumed, ΔS° is negative, so most lines slope upward (ΔG° becomes less negative with rising T). (b) The slope changes (a kink) at the melting or boiling point of the metal or oxide because ΔS° changes. (c) For C + O2 → CO2 the line is almost horizontal (ΔS° ≈ 0); for 2C + O2 → 2CO the line slopes downward (ΔS° > 0, more gas is produced) and crosses the other lines.

Interpretation: The lower a metal's line, the more negative its ΔG°, and the more stable its oxide. A metal can reduce the oxide of any metal whose line lies above it at that temperature, because the coupled reaction has a negative ΔG°.

Reducing agent selection: Carbon can reduce an oxide above a certain temperature where the C → CO line falls below the metal-oxide line (e.g. ZnO, FeO, SnO2 by coke at high temperature). Al and Mg lie low in the diagram and so reduce Cr2O3, Fe2O3 (thermite). Oxides at the very bottom (Al2O3, MgO, CaO) cannot be reduced by carbon at practical temperatures and are extracted by electrolysis. Noble metal oxides (Ag, Hg) decompose on heating (ΔG° becomes positive).
Use: the diagram tells the minimum temperature for smelting and the most economical reductant for each ore.

rubric.point: Labelled diagram: cation exchanger column, anion exchanger column, inlet/outlet
Cation exchange resin (R–H) reactions for Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>
Anion exchange resin (R′–OH) reactions for Cl<sup>−</sup>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>
Regeneration with dil. HCl/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and dil. NaOH with reactions
Merits over zeolite process (at least two) / demerits

answer: Principle: Ion-exchange (demineralisation) resins are insoluble, cross-linked organic polymers (styrene–divinylbenzene) bearing replaceable ionic groups. Cation exchangers (R–H) replace all cations by H+; anion exchangers (R′–OH) replace all anions by OH−; H+ and OH− combine to form water, giving demineralised (deionised) water.
Cation exchange resin (RH): strongly acidic, with –SO3H or –COOH groups (e.g. sulphonated polystyrene).
Anion exchange resin (R′OH): basic, with quaternary ammonium (–NR3OH) or amino groups.
Process: Hard water first passes down the cation exchange column, then the anion exchange column.

Cation exchanger: 2RH + Ca<sup>2+</sup> → R<sub>2</sub>Ca + 2H<sup>+</sup>; 2RH + Mg<sup>2+</sup> → R<sub>2</sub>Mg + 2H<sup>+</sup>; RH + Na<sup>+</sup> → RNa + H<sup>+</sup>. The effluent contains free acids (HCl, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>).

Anion exchanger: R′OH + Cl<sup>−</sup> → R′Cl + OH<sup>−</sup>; 2R′OH + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> → R′<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2OH<sup>−</sup>; R′OH + HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> → R′HCO<sub>3</sub> + OH<sup>−</sup>.
Net: H<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>O; the water leaving is free from all ions (hardness ≈ 0, pH ≈ 7). A degasser may remove CO<sub>2</sub>.

Regeneration: Exhausted cation exchanger is washed with dil. HCl or H2SO4: R2Ca + 2H+ → 2RH + Ca2+. Exhausted anion exchanger is washed with dil. NaOH: R′2SO4 + 2OH− → 2R′OH + SO42−. The washings are drained off.

Merits over zeolite process: (i) removes all ions (cations and anions), giving water of very low TDS, whereas zeolite replaces only Ca2+/Mg2+ by Na+; (ii) suitable for high-pressure boilers; (iii) works on acidic or turbid-free water over a wide pH range and does not add Na+; (iv) the process can be controlled to give water of very low hardness (0–2 ppm).
Demerits: costly equipment and resins; water must be free from turbidity and iron/manganese; skilled operation required.

rubric.point: Electrochemical theory: anodic and cathodic areas on iron surface, local cells, electrolyte film
Anode reaction Fe → Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>
(i) Hydrogen evolution: cathodic reaction 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → H<sub>2</sub> and overall reaction in acid
(ii) Oxygen absorption: ½O<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>−</sup> → 2OH<sup>−</sup>, Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> formation
Formation of rust Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>·xH<sub>2</sub>O by oxidation of Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> and diagram

answer: Electrochemical theory of wet corrosion: When iron is in contact with moisture/electrolyte and oxygen, different parts of the surface (due to impurities, strain, differences in concentration) behave as anodic and cathodic areas. A large number of tiny galvanic cells form: the anode is oxidised (corrodes), electrons flow through the metal to the cathode where a reduction reaction occurs, and ions move through the electrolyte film to complete the circuit.
Anodic reaction (oxidation, common to both): Fe → Fe2+ + 2e−. Corrosion takes place at the anode.

(i) Hydrogen evolution mechanism (acidic medium, absence of oxygen, pH < 5): Cathode: 2H+ + 2e− → H2↑. Overall: Fe + 2H+ → Fe2+ + H2. It occurs for metals above hydrogen in the electrochemical series and is favoured by acids; the cathode area is relatively small and the anode large.

(ii) Oxygen absorption mechanism (neutral or alkaline medium, with dissolved oxygen): Cathode: ½O2 + H2O + 2e− → 2OH−. Fe2+ from the anode and OH− from the cathode meet to give Fe(OH)2: Fe2+ + 2OH− → Fe(OH)2. Overall: Fe + ½O2 + H2O → Fe(OH)2.

Formation of rust: In the presence of excess oxygen, ferrous hydroxide is further oxidised: 4Fe(OH)2 + O2 + 2H2O → 4Fe(OH)3, which loses water to form yellow-brown rust, Fe2O3·xH2O. If oxygen is limited, black magnetite Fe3O4 forms.

Rust is porous and flaky, so it does not protect the underlying metal, and corrosion continues. Corrosion occurs at the anode (e.g. under a water drop centre/crevice where oxygen is poor), while rust deposits at the oxygen-rich cathodic region.
Conclusion: Oxygen absorption is the more common mechanism in natural waters and moist air; hydrogen evolution is important in acid environments such as pickling baths.

rubric.point: Any three differences between dry and wet corrosion (medium, mechanism, nature of products, rate)
Effect of temperature
Effect of pH
Effect of humidity

answer: Differences: (1) Medium: dry corrosion occurs by direct chemical attack of dry gases (O2, Cl2, SO2) in absence of moisture; wet corrosion needs a conducting liquid/electrolyte (moisture).
(2) Mechanism: dry corrosion follows adsorption and chemical (oxide-film) reaction – no electrochemical cells; wet corrosion follows an electrochemical mechanism with anodic and cathodic areas.

(3) Products: dry – corrosion products (oxide, sulphide, halide film) form at the surface and can be protective (Al2O3, Cr2O3); wet – products (rust) form between anode and cathode, are porous and non-protective.
(4) Rate: dry corrosion is slow and uniform; wet corrosion is rapid and localised (pitting, crevice, galvanic). (5) Wet corrosion is far more common (rusting, tarnishing).

Effect of temperature: the rate of corrosion generally increases with temperature (higher reaction rate, greater diffusion and ionic conductivity); however, at higher temperature the solubility of oxygen in water falls, and a protective oxide film may form.

Effect of pH: acidic medium (pH < 4) increases corrosion of most metals through hydrogen evolution; neutral to mildly alkaline medium (pH 7–10) with oxygen gives moderate corrosion; strongly alkaline medium forms a passive film on iron and reduces corrosion (amphoteric metals such as Al, Zn corrode in strong alkali).

Effect of humidity: moisture is required for the electrolyte film; above a critical humidity (about 60 % for iron) corrosion rate increases sharply, aided by hygroscopic salts and pollutants (SO2, NaCl), which form conducting films.

rubric.point: Principle of cathodic protection: forcing the metal to act as cathode
Sacrificial anode method: principle, working, anode materials (Mg, Zn, Al), applications
Impressed current method: DC source, inert anode (graphite, Pt, high-silicon iron), backfill, applications
Diagrams of both methods
Tabular comparison (at least three points)

answer: Principle: Corrosion is prevented by converting the whole metal structure into a cathode, so that no oxidation (M → Mn+ + ne−) can occur on it. Electrons are supplied either by a more active metal or by an external DC source.

1. Sacrificial anode (galvanic) protection: The structure to be protected (pipeline, ship hull, underground tank) is connected by a wire to a block of a more active metal (Mg, Zn or Al), which has a lower reduction potential than iron. The active metal acts as anode and gets corroded (sacrificed), while iron becomes the cathode and is protected.

Anode: Mg → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>; cathode (iron): O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e<sup>−</sup> → 4OH<sup>−</sup>. The consumed anodes are replaced periodically. Uses: buried pipelines, ship hulls, boilers, water tanks, small installations.

2. Impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP): The structure is connected to the negative terminal of an external DC source (rectifier), and an inert anode (graphite, platinised titanium, high-silicon iron, scrap iron) buried in the soil in coke-breeze backfill is connected to the positive terminal. The impressed current flows from the anode through soil to the structure, making it cathodic.

Anode reaction at the inert anode: 2H<sub>2</sub>O → O<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 4e<sup>−</sup> (or 2Cl<sup>−</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup>). Uses: large structures such as long pipelines, underground cables, marine piers, ships' hulls and storage tanks.

Comparison: (a) Power: sacrificial – no external power; ICCP – needs DC supply. (b) Anode: sacrificial – consumable active metal; ICCP – inert/slowly consumed anode. (c) Cost: sacrificial – low installation cost, higher replacement; ICCP – higher installation, lower running cost per unit area. (d) Current: sacrificial – small and fixed; ICCP – large and adjustable. (e) Suitability: sacrificial for small/short-term structures, ICCP for large, well-coated structures and high resistivity soils.
Q3.4.diagram: (a) Underground iron pipe connected by wire to a buried Mg block (arrow: electrons Mg → pipe). (b) Pipe connected to the − terminal of a DC rectifier; the + terminal connected to a graphite anode in coke backfill; arrows show current direction through the soil.

rubric.point: Sacrificial (anodic) coating – galvanizing: definition, example, protection even at breaks
Noble (cathodic) coating – tinning: example and behaviour at pores/cracks
Differences in a table
Methods of metallic coating: hot dipping, electroplating, cladding, cementation/sherardizing, metal spraying (any four)

answer: Anodic (sacrificial) coating – galvanizing: iron is coated with zinc, a metal more active (anodic) than iron. Zn protects iron even if the coating is broken, because zinc becomes the anode and is corroded while iron remains the cathode. Used for roofing sheets, buckets, wires, pipes.

Cathodic (noble) coating – tinning: iron is coated with a less active (more noble) metal such as tin, Ni, Cu or Cr. As long as the coating is intact, it protects; but if a pore or crack appears, iron becomes the anode, the small anodic area meets a large cathode and corrosion is rapid and concentrated. Used for food containers (tin cans), since tin is non-toxic.

Differences: (a) Zn is anodic to Fe, Sn is cathodic to Fe. (b) Galvanized iron is protected at breaks; tin-plated iron corrodes faster at breaks. (c) Galvanized containers cannot be used for acidic foods (Zn is toxic and attacked); tinned cans are used for food storage.

Methods of applying metallic coatings: (1) Hot dipping: the base metal is dipped in a molten bath of the coating metal (galvanizing in molten Zn, tinning in molten Sn). (2) Electroplating: the article is made the cathode in a bath containing the salt of the coating metal. (3) Cladding: a thin sheet of the coating metal is bonded by rolling or pressing (e.g. duralumin clad with Al). (4) Cementation (sherardizing, calorizing, chromizing): the article is heated in a powder of Zn, Al or Cr. (5) Metal spraying: molten metal is sprayed on the surface with a spray gun.

rubric.point: Principle: treatment with Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> and Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> to convert soluble Ca/Mg salts into insoluble CaCO<sub>3</sub> and Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>
Reactions for temporary hardness (Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, Mg(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) with lime
Reactions for permanent hardness (CaCl<sub>2</sub>, CaSO<sub>4</sub>, MgCl<sub>2</sub>, MgSO<sub>4</sub>) with lime and soda
Cold lime-soda process: working conditions, coagulant, residual hardness 50–60 ppm
Hot lime-soda process: temperature 80–150 °C, advantages, residual hardness 15–30 ppm
Diagram/flow or comparison table and statement of advantages

answer: Principle: Hardness-causing Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions are converted into insoluble CaCO3 and Mg(OH)2 by adding calculated amounts of lime Ca(OH)2 and soda ash Na2CO3. The precipitates settle and are removed by filtration (sludge).
Temporary hardness (removed by lime): Ca(HCO3)2 + Ca(OH)2 → 2CaCO3↓ + 2H2O; Mg(HCO3)2 + 2Ca(OH)2 → 2CaCO3↓ + Mg(OH)2↓ + 2H2O.
Permanent hardness – Mg salts (lime then soda): MgCl2 + Ca(OH)2 → Mg(OH)2↓ + CaCl2; MgSO4 + Ca(OH)2 → Mg(OH)2↓ + CaSO4. The CaCl2/CaSO4 so formed (and the original Ca salts) are removed by soda:
Permanent hardness – Ca salts (soda): CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3↓ + 2NaCl; CaSO4 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3↓ + Na2SO4. Also CO2/H+ or free acid present consumes lime: CO2 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 + H2O.

Cold lime-soda process: The calculated amounts of lime and soda are mixed with water at room temperature in a continuous tank with a stirrer; a coagulant (alum, sodium aluminate) is added so that the fine precipitates settle. Sludge settles in the conical bottom and softened water is filtered. Residual hardness ≈ 50–60 ppm.

Hot lime-soda process: The process is carried out at 80–150 °C with a mixture of water, lime and soda heated by steam. Reaction is fast, precipitate settles quickly and coagulant is not needed; dissolved gases are expelled and viscosity falls so filtration is easy. Residual hardness is lower, 15–30 ppm.

Comparison: hot process – faster, no coagulant, more efficient, costly equipment; cold process – slow, needs coagulant, simple and cheap. Both processes are economical and increase the pH of water, reducing corrosion; the drawback is the disposal of large amounts of sludge.

rubric.point: Natural osmosis vs reverse osmosis definition with osmotic pressure
Principle: applying pressure greater than osmotic pressure to the saline side
Labelled diagram of RO cell with semi-permeable membrane
Working, membrane materials (cellulose acetate, polyamide), pressure 15–40 kg/cm<sup>2</sup>
Differences from natural osmosis and merits/uses

answer: Osmosis is the spontaneous flow of solvent from a dilute solution (or pure solvent) to a concentrated solution through a semi-permeable membrane (SPM). The pressure that just prevents this flow is the osmotic pressure π (π = CRT).

Reverse osmosis: When a hydrostatic pressure larger than the osmotic pressure is applied on the concentrated (saline) side, the flow of solvent is reversed: pure water passes from the concentrated side to the dilute side, leaving the dissolved salts behind.

Set-up: A pressure vessel is divided by a semi-permeable membrane (cellulose acetate, polyamide or polysulfone thin-film composite in spiral-wound modules). Hard/saline water is pumped to the feed side at 15–40 kg cm−2 (up to ≈ 60–70 bar for sea water) after filtration.

Working: Water molecules pass through the pores, while Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, Cl−, SO42−, bacteria, colloids and dissolved organics (≈ 95–99 % of dissolved solids) are rejected; the concentrated reject (brine) is drained off. Hence both softening and desalination are achieved.

Difference from natural osmosis: (a) Direction – RO: solvent moves from concentrated to dilute side; osmosis: dilute to concentrated. (b) Pressure – RO needs applied pressure > π; osmosis is spontaneous. (c) RO is a forced, energy-consuming process used for purification; osmosis is a natural process.

Advantages: removes ionic and non-ionic, colloidal and bacterial impurities; low cost of operation, membrane can be replaced quickly; compact, no regeneration chemicals. Used in desalination of sea/brackish water, in drinking water plants, boiler feed and pharmaceutical industries.
Limitation: membrane fouling and scaling, high pressure/energy, wastage of reject water.

rubric.point: Principle: temporary hardness only, addition of calculated amount of lime Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>
Reaction for Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> and Mg(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>
Procedure and removal of precipitate; point that excess lime must be avoided
Limitation/application

answer: Clark's process (lime process) removes only temporary hardness (bicarbonates of Ca and Mg). Calculated amount of slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, is added to hard water, which converts soluble bicarbonates into insoluble CaCO3 and Mg(OH)2.
Ca(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → 2CaCO<sub>3</sub>↓ + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
Mg(HCO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → 2CaCO<sub>3</sub>↓ + Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>↓ + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
Free CO<sub>2</sub> in the water is also removed: CO<sub>2</sub> + Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> → CaCO<sub>3</sub>↓ + H<sub>2</sub>O.

Procedure: The measured lime is mixed with the water in a tank, stirred and allowed to settle; the precipitated CaCO3 and Mg(OH)2 are filtered off. The quantity of lime must be exact: excess lime itself makes the water hard (and caustic).
Limitation: permanent hardness (chlorides, sulphates) is not removed; hence it is used as a first step for water containing mainly temporary hardness.

rubric.point: Definition of hardness; temporary vs permanent hardness salts
Differences (removal by boiling, salts, other names, softening methods) in tabular form
Causes of hardness (dissolved Ca/Mg salts from rocks, CO<sub>2</sub> in rain water etc.)
Effects of hardness (domestic and industrial, boilers, textile, paper etc.)
Why hard water consumes more soap: reactions forming scum

answer: Hardness is the soap-destroying power of water, caused by dissolved bicarbonates, chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (and Fe, Mn, Al salts).
Temporary (carbonate) hardness: due to bicarbonates of Ca and Mg. It is removed by boiling: Ca(HCO3)2 → CaCO3↓ + H2O + CO2↑; Mg(HCO3)2 → Mg(OH)2↓ + 2CO2↑.
Permanent (non-carbonate) hardness: due to chlorides and sulphates of Ca and Mg (CaCl2, MgCl2, CaSO4, MgSO4). It is not removed by boiling; it needs lime-soda, zeolite, or ion exchange treatment.

Differences: (1) salts – bicarbonates vs chlorides/sulphates; (2) boiling removes the first, not the second; (3) temporary hardness can also be removed by Clark's process, permanent only by chemical methods; (4) temporary hardness causes scale/sludge by decomposition, permanent hardness causes scales at the high temperature of boilers (CaSO4) due to decreased solubility.

Causes: Rain water dissolves CO2 from air and soil to form carbonic acid, which attacks limestone, dolomite and gypsum on its way, bringing Ca2+, Mg2+, HCO3−, Cl− and SO42− into ground and river water: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 → Ca(HCO3)2.

Effects: (a) Domestic: wastage of soap, scum on clothes, bad taste, poor cooking of pulses/vegetables, scaling of kettles. (b) Industrial: boiler scale and sludge, corrosion, reduced efficiency and risk of explosions; in textile and dyeing industries poor dyeing and spots; in paper and sugar industries impure product; in pharmaceutical industry contamination.

Soap consumption: Soap is sodium/potassium salt of higher fatty acid (e.g. sodium stearate, C17H35COONa). Ca2+ and Mg2+ react with it to give insoluble scum: 2C17H35COONa + CaCl2 → (C17H35COO)2Ca↓ + 2NaCl; 2C17H35COONa + MgSO4 → (C17H35COO)2Mg↓ + Na2SO4.
Lather is formed only after all Ca<sup>2+</sup>/Mg<sup>2+</sup> have been precipitated; thus a large quantity of soap is wasted before cleaning can start.

rubric.point: Differences between sludge and scale (any three)
Calgon conditioning: formula Na<sub>2</sub>[Na<sub>4</sub>(PO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>] and reaction forming soluble complex [Na<sub>2</sub>Ca<sub>2</sub>(PO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]
Why Calgon is superior (soluble complex, no sludge, no pH problem, easy to use)

answer: Sludge is a soft, loose, slimy precipitate (MgCO3, MgCl2, CaCl2, MgSO4) formed in colder parts of the boiler; it is a poor conductor of heat, but is easily removed by blow-down. Scale is a hard, adherent coating (CaSO4, CaCO3, Mg(OH)2, silica) on the inner walls at the hottest parts; it is removed with difficulty (scraping, thermal shock, chemical treatment) and causes fuel wastage, overheating and explosions.
Calgon conditioning: Calgon is sodium hexametaphosphate, Na2[Na4(PO3)6]. It is added to the boiler water, where it reacts with Ca2+ to form a highly soluble complex ion, which does not precipitate:

2CaSO<sub>4</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>[Na<sub>4</sub>(PO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>] → Na<sub>2</sub>[Ca<sub>2</sub>(PO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>] + 2Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (the Ca<sup>2+</sup> is held in a soluble complex anion, so scale is prevented).

Superiority over phosphate/carbonate conditioning: (i) no insoluble sludge or scale of calcium phosphate/carbonate is produced; the complex is soluble and passes out with the blow-down; (ii) it also dissolves the scale already present; (iii) it works over a wide pH range and does not need maintaining a precise alkalinity (phosphate conditioning needs pH 9–10); (iv) the quantity of treatment is small and the process is simple and economical.

rubric.point: Implications of hard water in boilers: scale and sludge, corrosion, caustic embrittlement, priming and foaming (any four)
Priming: definition and cause
Foaming: definition and cause
Prevention of priming and foaming

answer: Implications: (1) Scale and sludge formation: reduced heat transfer, fuel wastage, overheating of tubes and explosion risk; clogging of pipes. (2) Corrosion: dissolved O2, CO2 and acid produced by MgCl2 hydrolysis (MgCl2 + 2H2O → Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl) attack boiler metal. (3) Caustic embrittlement: NaOH from Na2CO3 hydrolysis causes cracks at stressed joints. (4) Priming and foaming cause wet steam and carry-over. (5) Decrease in boiler life and efficiency.

Priming: the production of wet steam when a boiler is steamed very rapidly, so that tiny droplets of water are carried along with the steam. Causes: very high water level, sudden boiling, high steam velocity, defective boiler design, large amount of dissolved solids.

Foaming: the formation of a persistent foam or bubbles at the water surface which do not break easily. Causes: presence of oil, grease and suspended impurities and surface-active agents (soaps, detergents), which lower surface tension.

Prevention: Priming – maintain a proper water level, avoid sudden steaming, use steam purifiers/baffles, soften water to reduce dissolved solids, blow-down regularly. Foaming – remove oil by adding sodium aluminate or anti-foaming agents (castor oil, synthetic polyamides), and remove oil and suspended solids from feed water by blow-down and filtering.

rubric.point: Definition of alkalinity (acid-neutralising capacity)
Causes of alkalinity (OH<sup>−</sup>, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>) and their combinations
Determination by titration with standard H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> using phenolphthalein (P) and methyl orange (M) indicators
Reactions and calculation table P, M (OH<sup>−</sup>, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>)

answer: Alkalinity of water is its capacity to neutralise acid; it is expressed in ppm or mg/L as CaCO3.

Causes: presence of hydroxide (OH−), carbonate (CO32−) and bicarbonate (HCO3−) ions, formed by dissolution of rocks, CO2, and by the addition of lime/soda in softening. OH− and HCO3− cannot exist together because OH− + HCO3− → CO32− + H2O. Possible combinations: OH− alone; CO32− alone; HCO3− alone; OH− + CO32−; CO32− + HCO3−.

Determination: A known volume (e.g. 100 mL) of water is titrated with standard N/50 H2SO4. First with phenolphthalein indicator until the pink colour disappears (end point P: neutralises all OH− and half the CO32−: OH− + H+ → H2O; CO32− + H+ → HCO3−). Then methyl orange is added and the titration continued to the red/orange end point (total M: HCO3− + H+ → H2O + CO2).

Calculation (P and M in mL of acid): P = 0, M > 0 → only HCO3− = M; P = ½M → only CO32− = 2P; P = M → only OH− = P; P < ½M → CO32− = 2P and HCO3− = M − 2P; P > ½M → OH− = 2P − M and CO32− = 2(M − P). Alkalinity (ppm as CaCO3) = (volume × normality × 50 × 1000)/(volume of sample).

Identifying which impurities need lime and/or soda (formula with 74/100 and 106/100)

rubric.point: Principle: complete combustion of a known mass of fuel at constant volume in excess O<sub>2</sub> in a closed bomb; heat absorbed by water
Labelled diagram of bomb calorimeter
Construction (stainless steel bomb, crucible, ignition wire, oxygen inlet, calorimeter, stirrer, Beckmann thermometer, air jacket)
Working procedure: 1 g fuel, 25 atm O<sub>2</sub>, ignition, temperature rise
Formula for GCV and NCV (NCV = GCV − 0.09H × 587)
Corrections: fuse wire, acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), cooling/radiation

answer: Principle: A known mass of the fuel is burnt completely in excess oxygen at constant volume inside a closed steel bomb, which is immersed in a known mass of water. The heat liberated is absorbed by the water and the calorimeter; from the rise in temperature, the calorific value is calculated. Since products are cooled to the initial temperature, the steam condenses and the value found is the Gross (higher) calorific value.

Construction: (i) A strong stainless-steel bomb with a gas-tight screw lid, provided with an oxygen inlet valve and two electrodes; (ii) a small ignition (nickel/platinum) crucible supported on one electrode; a fine fuse wire connects the electrodes and touches the fuel; (iii) the bomb is placed in a copper calorimeter containing a known weight of water, fitted with a stirrer and a Beckmann thermometer; (iv) an outer air jacket and water jacket minimise heat loss.

Working: About 0.5–1 g of the fuel (pelletised if solid) is weighed in the crucible, the fuse wire is arranged, and the bomb is filled with pure oxygen at about 25 atm. It is placed in the water of the calorimeter, and the initial steady temperature t1 is noted. The fuel is ignited electrically; combustion is rapid, the stirrer is operated and the maximum temperature t2 is recorded.

Calculation: Let x = mass of fuel, W = mass of water, w = water equivalent of calorimeter and bomb, Δt = (t2 − t1) with corrections. Then heat gained = (W + w)Δt, so GCV = (W + w)(t2 − t1 + tc) − (fuse + acid corrections) / x (cal/g or kcal/kg).

Corrections: (1) Fuse wire correction – heat produced by burning of the ignition wire is subtracted. (2) Acid correction – nitrogen and sulphur in the fuel oxidise to HNO3 and H2SO4 under high pressure, liberating extra heat (formation of HNO3 57.6 kcal/mol, H2SO4 144 kcal/mol), which must be subtracted. (3) Cooling (radiation) correction – heat lost by radiation during the experiment is added to the observed rise of temperature (tc, found from the cooling rate). (4) Also the sensitivity of the thermometer and heat of ignition pellets may be corrected.
Net calorific value: NCV = GCV − latent heat of steam formed = GCV − 0.09 H × 587 cal/g (H = % hydrogen; 587 cal/g is the latent heat of steam; 1 g H gives 9 g H2O).
Use: accurate determination of the calorific value of solid and non-volatile liquid fuels (coal, coke, fuel oil).

rubric.point: Definition of conducting polymer (conjugated π-electron backbone)
Classification: intrinsically conducting (conjugated, doped) and extrinsically conducting (conducting-element filled, blended)
Structures of polyacetylene, polyaniline, polypyrrole/polythiophene
p-type doping (oxidative) with I<sub>2</sub>/AsF<sub>5</sub> – mechanism with polaron/bipolaron
n-type doping (reductive) with Na/Li – mechanism
Applications (at least four)

answer: Conducting polymers are organic polymers that conduct electricity. Ordinary polymers are insulators, but polymers having a backbone of alternate single and double bonds (conjugated π-system) become conducting when doped.

Classification: (1) Intrinsically conducting polymers – conductivity arises from the conjugated π electrons of the polymer backbone. (a) Conjugated polymers: polyacetylene (–CH=CH–)n, polyaniline, polypyrrole, polythiophene, poly(p-phenylene vinylene). (b) Doped polymers obtained from the above by oxidation/reduction. (2) Extrinsically conducting polymers – an insulating polymer filled with conducting material such as carbon black, metal fibres or oxides (conducting-element filled) or blended with a conducting polymer.

Structure: polyacetylene –CH=CH–CH=CH–; polyaniline: alternating benzenoid–amine and quinoid–imine units (–C6H4–NH–C6H4–N=); polypyrrole and polythiophene: five-membered rings (N–H or S) linked at 2,5 positions. The extended π-orbitals overlap to give bands, but with a band gap, so undoped polymer is a semiconductor/insulator.
Doping: Conductivity is raised (from 10−10 to about 103–105 S cm−1) by introducing charge carriers via redox doping.

p-doping (oxidative): The polymer is treated with an oxidising agent such as I2, Br2, AsF5 or FeCl3. An electron is removed from the π-bond, creating a positive hole (radical cation, polaron/bipolaron) delocalised along the chain: (CH)n + (3x/2)I2 → [(CH)x+]n + xI3−. These holes move through the chain under a potential, giving conduction.

n-doping (reductive): Treatment with a reducing agent such as sodium naphthalide, Li or Na adds electrons to the π* band, forming carbanions (negative charge carriers): (CH)n + xNa → [(CH)x−]n + xNa+. The charges migrate along the chain. n-doped polymers are less stable in air.

Applications: rechargeable lightweight batteries, electrochromic displays and smart windows, organic light-emitting diodes (OLED), solar cells, sensors and biosensors, antistatic coatings and EMI shielding, corrosion protection coatings, artificial muscles/actuators, transistors and microelectronic devices.

Uses: lenses, aircraft windows and canopies, display signs, dentures, bone cement, light covers.

(ii) PAN (polyacrylonitrile, Orlon/Acrilan): Preparation: free-radical polymerisation of acrylonitrile CH2=CH–CN: n CH2=CHCN → [–CH2–CH(CN)–]n. Properties: high tensile strength, polar, resistant to solvents and sunlight, high melting point. Uses: acrylic fibres (wool substitute, blankets, sweaters), precursor of carbon fibre, membranes.

Properties: high tensile strength, crystalline, low moisture absorption, resistant to chemicals. Uses: textile fibres (Terylene), bottles, films, tyre cords, packaging.

Properties: elastic, tough, abrasion and chemical resistant. Uses: foams (cushions, mattresses), insulation, paints, adhesives, elastic fibres (spandex), shoe soles.

(vi) Buna-S (SBR): copolymer of butadiene (75 %) and styrene (25 %), emulsion polymerisation with free-radical initiator at 5 °C (cold rubber). Properties: good abrasion resistance, ageing resistance, but poor oil resistance; vulcanised with S. Uses: tyres, footwear soles, floor tiles, cables. Buna-N (NBR): copolymer of butadiene and acrylonitrile (CH2=CH–CN) by emulsion polymerisation. Properties: excellent resistance to oils, petrol and solvents. rubric.point: Addition polymerisation: definition, example (ethylene → polyethylene), free-radical mechanism with initiation, propagation, termination steps
Condensation polymerisation: definition, mechanism (step-wise reaction with elimination of small molecules), examples (Nylon-6,6, PET, Bakelite)
Differences between chain-growth and step-growth (at least four points)

answer: Addition (chain-growth) polymerisation: Monomers containing a double bond (vinyl type) add to one another repeatedly to form a polymer without loss of any small molecule. The polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. Example: n CH2=CH2 → [–CH2–CH2–]n.

Free-radical mechanism: (1) Initiation: peroxide (R–O–O–R) → 2RO•; RO• + CH2=CH2 → RO–CH2–CH2•. (2) Propagation: RO–CH2–CH2• + CH2=CH2 → RO–(CH2–CH2)2• → … → RO–(CH2CH2)n•. (3) Termination: by coupling of two growing chains, 2 R(CH2CH2)n• → R(CH2CH2)2nR, or by disproportionation. Other examples: PVC, polystyrene, PTFE, polypropylene. Ionic (cationic/anionic) and coordination mechanisms also exist.

Condensation (step-growth) polymerisation: Bifunctional (or polyfunctional) monomers react with each other, with the elimination of small molecules such as H2O, HCl or CH3OH at each step. The polymer repeat unit differs from the monomers.

Mechanism: A dimer forms first (e.g. diamine + diacid → amide + H2O), the dimer reacts further with monomers or other dimers to form trimers, tetramers and finally long chains: H2N–R–NH2 + HOOC–R′–COOH → H2N–R–NHCO–R′–COOH + H2O → … → [–NH–R–NHCO–R′–CO–]n. Examples: Nylon-6,6, PET (terephthalic acid + ethylene glycol), Bakelite (phenol + formaldehyde), polycarbonate.

Chain-growth vs step-growth: (1) Monomers: unsaturated (C=C) vs bifunctional with reactive groups (–OH, –COOH, –NH2). (2) Growth: by successive addition of monomer to an active centre (radical/ion) vs reaction between any two species (monomer–monomer, oligomer–oligomer). (3) High molecular mass formed quickly even at low conversion vs high molecular mass reached only at very high conversion (>99 %). (4) By-products: none vs small molecules like H2O eliminated. (5) Monomer disappears slowly; reaction mixture contains monomer and high polymer vs monomer disappears very early. (6) Needs initiator/catalyst, is exothermic and rapid vs generally slower, heat is needed.

rubric.point: Tacticity: definition
Isotactic, syndiotactic and atactic arrangements with diagrams and example (polypropylene) and properties
Functionality: definition and degree of polymerisation relation
Why methanol does not polymerise (functionality = 1)

answer: Tacticity is the spatial arrangement of the substituent groups (R) on the asymmetric carbon atoms along the polymer backbone [–CH2–CHR–]n.

Isotactic: all R groups lie on the same side of the chain (all above the plane of the zig-zag backbone). The chain is regular, packs well, and the polymer is highly crystalline, strong, high-melting (e.g. isotactic polypropylene by Ziegler–Natta catalyst).
Syndiotactic: R groups lie alternately on opposite sides of the chain; stereoregular, crystalline, with properties between isotactic and atactic.
Atactic: R groups are arranged randomly on both sides; the chain is irregular, amorphous, soft, low-melting and sticky (e.g. atactic polypropylene obtained by free-radical polymerisation).

Functionality of a monomer is the number of bonding sites (reactive functional groups) through which it can link to other monomers. A monomer with functionality 2 (bifunctional: ethylene by its double bond, glycol, adipic acid) gives linear polymers, functionality 3 (glycerol, phenol) gives cross-linked polymers.

Methanol (CH3OH) has only one reactive group (–OH); its functionality is 1. It can form only a dimer (CH3OCH3), and further growth is blocked because the molecule has no second site to continue chain growth. A monomer must be at least bifunctional to polymerise.

rubric.point: Definition of lubrication and functions
Classification: solid, semi-solid (greases), liquid (oils); and synthetic/emulsions
Fluid-film (hydrodynamic) lubrication mechanism with diagram
Boundary lubrication mechanism
Extreme-pressure lubrication mechanism with additives (chlorinated, sulphurised, phosphated compounds)

answer: Lubrication is the process of reducing friction and wear between two moving surfaces by interposing a substance (lubricant) between them. Functions: reduce friction and wear, carry away heat, prevent corrosion, act as a seal, remove dirt and increase efficiency.

Classification of lubricants: (1) Liquid lubricants (oils): animal/vegetable oils (castor, palm), mineral/petroleum oils, synthetic oils (silicones, polyglycols) and blended oils. (2) Semi-solid lubricants (greases): mixture of oil with soap (Ca, Na, Li soap) as thickener. (3) Solid lubricants: graphite, molybdenum disulphide, talc, boron nitride, PTFE. Also emulsions and aerosols.

(i) Fluid film (hydrodynamic) lubrication: The two moving surfaces are completely separated by a thick film of fluid (at least 1000 Å), so metal-to-metal contact is avoided. Friction arises only from the internal resistance (viscosity) of the fluid. It is achieved with low-viscosity oils in journal bearings, where rotation draws oil into a wedge-shaped film that supports the load. Friction coefficient is very low (0.001–0.03); the film thickness depends on viscosity, speed and load.

(ii) Boundary (thin film) lubrication: Under heavy load or low speed or high temperature, the fluid film is squeezed out or discontinuous. A thin film of lubricant (a few molecular layers) is adsorbed on the metal surfaces by physical or chemical adsorption (polar groups such as fatty acids, esters, soaps), preventing direct contact of asperities. Lubricants: vegetable oils, fatty acids, graphite, MoS2, greases. Used in gears, cams, piston rings.

(iii) Extreme pressure (EP) lubrication: At very high loads, speeds and temperatures (hypoid gears, cutting tools, rolling mills), ordinary films break down. EP additives such as chlorinated esters, sulphurised oils, tricresyl phosphate react chemically with the metal surfaces at the local high temperature to form durable films of metal chlorides, sulphides or phosphides (FeCl2, FeS, FePO4), with low shear strength and high melting point; these films prevent welding and seizure of the metal surfaces.
