rubric.point: Flash and fire point: definitions, apparatus (Pensky–Martens), significance
Cloud and pour point: definitions, significance
Aniline point: definition, significance (aromatic content, rubber/seal compatibility)
Viscosity index: definition, formula VI = (L − U)/(L − H) × 100, significance
Solid lubricant named (graphite or MoS<sub>2</sub>) and mechanism

answer: 1. Flash and fire point: The flash point is the lowest temperature at which the vapour of an oil gives a momentary flash when a small flame is brought near it under specified conditions; the fire point is the lowest temperature at which the vapours burn continuously for at least 5 seconds. Fire point is 5–40 °C higher than flash point. Determined by Pensky–Martens (closed cup) or Abel's apparatus. Significance: a lubricant must have a flash point well above the working temperature to prevent fire hazards; it also indicates volatility.

2. Cloud and pour point: The cloud point is the temperature at which the oil becomes cloudy or hazy owing to separation of waxes or solid crystals on cooling. The pour point is the temperature at which the oil ceases to flow when cooled (the lowest temperature at which it still pours). Pour point is lower than cloud point. Significance: they indicate suitability of the oil in cold climates and refrigeration machines; a lubricant must have a pour point lower than the lowest operating temperature to avoid blockage of oil passages.

3. Aniline point: The minimum temperature at which equal volumes of the oil and aniline become completely miscible. A low aniline point indicates high aromatic hydrocarbon content, which tends to dissolve/swell rubber seals and gaskets; a high aniline point indicates a paraffinic, rubber-safe oil. It gives an idea of the aromatic content and of the ignition quality (diesel index = aniline point °F × API gravity/100).

4. Viscosity index (VI): An empirical number showing the rate of change of viscosity with temperature. Oil of high VI shows small change of viscosity with temperature. It is calculated by comparing the oil with two reference oils (Pennsylvanian oil, VI = 100; Gulf oil, VI = 0) having the same viscosity at 210 °F: VI = (L − U)/(L − H) × 100, where U = viscosity of the test oil at 100 °F, L = viscosity of the VI 0 standard oil at 100 °F and H = viscosity of the VI 100 standard oil at 100 °F. Significance: a high VI oil is preferred for engines operating over wide temperature ranges.

Solid lubricant: graphite. It has a layered structure of hexagonal carbon sheets held together by weak van der Waals forces. The layers slide over one another under shear, reducing friction (like a pack of cards). Layers adsorb gases or moisture, which weakens interlayer forces. Used in the form of powder, in oil/water dispersion (oildag, aquadag), in high-temperature (up to 650 °C) and electrically conducting applications (motors, furnaces). (Alternative: MoS2 with similar layered structure.)

rubric.point: Definition of vulcanization (heating rubber with sulfur at 100–140 °C)
Chemistry: sulfur cross-links (–S–S– bridges) between polyisoprene chains at the double-bond/allylic sites, with diagram
Accelerators and fillers (ZnO, carbon black) and degree of vulcanization (3–5 % hard S gives soft rubber; 20–30 % gives ebonite)
Improvement in properties (tensile strength, elasticity, hardness, resistance to abrasion, solvents, oxidation, temperature)
Uses of vulcanized rubber

answer: Vulcanization is the process of heating raw (natural) rubber with sulfur (3–5 %) at 100–140 °C, in presence of an accelerator (ZBX, ZnO), to form sulfur cross-links between the long polyisoprene chains. It was discovered by Charles Goodyear in 1839.

Natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene, [–CH2–C(CH3)=CH–CH2–]n, whose chains coil and are held only by weak van der Waals forces. Raw rubber is soft, sticky, has low tensile strength, becomes plastic when hot and brittle when cold, absorbs water, swells in organic solvents and is attacked by oxidants.

Chemistry: Sulfur atoms add at the double bond sites (reactive α-methylene hydrogens) of the polyisoprene chains and form –S–S– (or –S–) bridges between adjacent chains, making a three-dimensional network: chain–CH–S–S–CH–chain. Sulfur is thus tied covalently across chains.
Extent of cross-linking: 3–5 % S gives soft, flexible rubber (tyre tubes); 10–15 % S gives semi-hard rubber; 30–32 % S gives hard, rigid, non-elastic ebonite.

Improvement in properties after vulcanization: (1) Higher tensile strength (up to 2000 kg cm−2) and elasticity since the cross-links resist slipping of chains and restore the original shape; (2) better resistance to abrasion, tear and wear; (3) lower water absorption; (4) increased resistance to solvents (swelling is limited by cross-links), oxidation and ozone; (5) wider useful temperature range (−40 to 100 °C) – rubber no longer becomes sticky when hot nor brittle when cold; (6) higher hardness and stiffness, and good electrical insulation.
Uses: tyres, tubes, conveyor belts, hoses, gaskets, shoe soles, shock absorbers, insulation of cables, ebonite for battery containers and electrical parts.

rubric.point: Stages of anaerobic digestion: hydrolysis, acidogenesis (acetogenesis), methanogenesis with reactions
Composition of biogas (CH<sub>4</sub> 55–65 %, CO<sub>2</sub> 30–40 %)
Environmental impact of biogas use (renewable, reduces methane emissions, residual slurry, CO<sub>2</sub>)
Causes and effects of air pollution (any two each)

answer: Biogas production is the anaerobic digestion of organic waste (cow dung, sewage, crop residues) by bacteria in a closed digester in absence of oxygen, in three main stages:

1. Hydrolysis: Hydrolytic bacteria secrete extracellular enzymes that break down complex polymers (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) into soluble monomers: sugars, amino acids and fatty acids. (C6H10O5)n + nH2O → nC6H12O6.

2. Acidogenesis (acid formation): Fermentative acid-forming bacteria convert the monomers into volatile fatty acids (acetic, propionic, butyric), alcohols, CO2 and H2; acetogenesis converts these to acetic acid: C6H12O6 → 3CH3COOH.

3. Methanogenesis: Methanogenic bacteria (Methanobacterium, Methanosarcina) produce methane: CH3COOH → CH4 + CO2 (aceticlastic); CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O. Biogas contains CH4 (55–65 %), CO2 (30–40 %), traces of H2S, H2, N2, with CV ≈ 5000–5500 kcal/m³.

Environmental impact of biogas: it is a renewable, clean-burning fuel with no soot or smoke (reducing indoor air pollution), recycles organic waste, prevents release of methane (a greenhouse gas about 25 times stronger than CO2) from decomposing waste and gives nutrient-rich slurry as manure; its combustion releases CO2, which is part of the short carbon cycle (carbon-neutral), unlike fossil fuels.

Air pollution – causes: burning of fossil fuels in vehicles and industry (CO, NOx, SO2, particulates), thermal power plants, biomass burning, chemical industries, CFCs. Effects: respiratory and cardiac diseases, acid rain (SO2, NOx), global warming (CO2, CH4), ozone layer depletion (CFC), photochemical smog and damage to buildings and crops.

rubric.point: Definition of viscosity index (empirical number showing rate of change of viscosity with temperature)

Correct identification: L = 800 s, H = 500 s, U = 600 s

answer: Viscosity index (VI) is an arbitrary number that measures how little the viscosity of a lubricating oil changes with temperature. A high VI means the oil's viscosity changes little with temperature (desirable). The reference scale: Pennsylvanian oil (least change) VI = 100, Gulf oil (greatest change) VI = 0.

Formula (Dean and Davis): VI = (L − U)/(L − H) × 100, where U = viscosity of the unknown oil at 100 °F, L = viscosity at 100 °F of the low-VI (Gulf) oil, H = viscosity at 100 °F of the high-VI (Pennsylvanian) oil; all three oils have the same viscosity (60 s) at 210 °F.
Conclusion: the oil's viscosity varies less than the Gulf standard but more than the Pennsylvanian standard, i.e. it has a moderate VI.

rubric.point: Principle: nuclei with spin I = ½ (<sup>1</sup>H) behave as tiny magnets; in field B<sub>0</sub> they split into two levels (α, β); resonance when hν = ΔE
Resonance condition ν = γB<sub>0</sub>/2π (radio-frequency absorption)
Shielding and deshielding explained with induced field / electron density
Definition of chemical shift δ = (ν<sub>sample</sub> − ν<sub>TMS</sub>)/ν<sub>spectrometer</sub> × 10<sup>6</sup> ppm
Reasons for using TMS as internal standard (any two)

answer: Principle: nuclei with non-zero spin (e.g. 1H, I = ½) possess a magnetic moment. In the absence of a field the two spin states (mI = +½, −½) are degenerate. In an external magnetic field B0 they split: the α state (aligned with the field, lower energy) and the β state (opposed, higher energy), with ΔE = γħB0.

When radio-frequency radiation of frequency ν is applied such that hν = ΔE, the nucleus absorbs energy and flips from α to β (resonance): ν = γB0/2π. The absorption is detected and plotted as an NMR spectrum. For a given nucleus the signal position depends on its chemical environment.

Shielding: the circulation of the electrons around a proton generates a small induced field opposing B0, so the proton experiences an effective field Beff = B0(1 − σ), slightly smaller than B0. High electron density (e.g. next to electron-donating groups) means greater shielding; the signal appears at lower δ (upfield).

Deshielding: electron-withdrawing groups (O, halogens, C=O) or π-electron ring currents (aromatic protons) reduce the electron density at the proton, so it feels a larger effective field and resonates at higher δ (downfield).

Chemical shift (δ): the position of a signal relative to a reference, expressed in ppm: δ = (νsample − νTMS) / (spectrometer frequency in MHz) = [(νsample − νTMS)/ν0] × 106. It is independent of the instrument's field strength.

Why TMS, Si(CH3)4, is used as internal standard: (i) all 12 protons are equivalent, giving a single sharp signal; (ii) silicon is electropositive, so the protons are highly shielded and its signal appears at δ = 0, upfield of almost all organic protons; (iii) chemically inert and does not react with the sample; (iv) volatile (b.p. 27 °C), so it is easily removed and the sample recovered; (v) soluble in most organic solvents.

rubric.point: Spin-spin coupling: splitting of a signal by non-equivalent neighbouring protons
n+1 rule with example (e.g. ethyl group: triplet + quartet)
Coupling constant J: spacing between split lines in Hz, independent of B<sub>0</sub>
Chemical shift definition with formula in ppm

answer: Spin-spin coupling: the magnetic field felt by a proton is modified by the spin states (α or β) of protons on adjacent carbon atoms (three bonds away, H–C–C–H). This splits a signal into a multiplet. A proton with n equivalent neighbouring protons gives n + 1 lines (n + 1 rule), with intensities from Pascal's triangle (1:1 doublet, 1:2:1 triplet, 1:3:3:1 quartet).

Example: in CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl the CH<sub>3</sub> protons (two neighbours) appear as a triplet and the CH<sub>2</sub> protons (three neighbours) as a quartet. Equivalent protons do not split one another.

Coupling constant (J): the distance in Hz between adjacent lines of a multiplet. It measures the strength of the coupling, is independent of the applied field B0, and the coupled partners have the same J. Typical vicinal J ≈ 6–8 Hz.
Chemical shift (δ): the position of a resonance signal relative to TMS: δ = [(νsample − νTMS)/ν0] × 106 ppm. It reflects the electronic environment (shielding/deshielding) of the proton.

rubric.point: S<sub>N</sub>2: one-step concerted mechanism with transition state shown
S<sub>N</sub>2 rate law (second order) and Walden inversion
S<sub>N</sub>1: two-step mechanism via carbocation
S<sub>N</sub>1 rate law (first order) and racemization
Tabular differentiation (substrate, solvent, nucleophile, leaving group etc.)

answer: Nucleophilic substitution: R–X + Nu− → R–Nu + X−; a nucleophile replaces a leaving group at an sp3 carbon.

SN2 (bimolecular) mechanism: a single concerted step. The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group (backside attack) while the C–X bond breaks. Pentacoordinate transition state: [Nu···C···X]δ− with the three other groups in a plane (sp2-like). Example: CH3Br + OH− → CH3OH + Br−.
Rate law: rate = k[R–X][Nu−] (second order). Stereochemistry: complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), like an umbrella turning inside out; (R) → (S) product.

SN1 (unimolecular) mechanism: two steps. Step 1 (slow, rate-determining): ionisation of the substrate to a planar carbocation, (CH3)3C–Br → (CH3)3C+ + Br−. Step 2 (fast): attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation, (CH3)3C+ + OH− → (CH3)3COH.

Rate law: rate = k[R–X] (first order, independent of [Nu]). Stereochemistry: the nucleophile can attack the planar carbocation from either face, giving a mixture of retention and inversion, i.e. racemization (partial in practice, because of ion-pair effects).

Differences: (i) SN2 is one step, SN1 two steps; (ii) kinetics second order vs first order; (iii) reactivity CH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° for SN2, but 3° > 2° > 1° for SN1 (carbocation stability); (iv) SN2 favoured by strong nucleophile and polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, acetone), SN1 by weak nucleophile and polar protic solvents (water, alcohol); (v) inversion vs racemization; (vi) no rearrangement in SN2, rearrangement possible in SN1; (vii) good leaving group needed in both.

rubric.point: Electronic spectroscopy defined (absorption of UV-Vis radiation causing electronic transitions, 200–800 nm)
Four transition types with relative energies and typical λ ranges
Shifts: bathochromic, hypsochromic, hyperchromic, hypochromic
Transitions in O<sub>2</sub>
Transitions in benzene

answer: Electronic spectroscopy (UV-Visible) deals with absorption of radiation of 200–800 nm by molecules, which promotes electrons from occupied ground-state orbitals (bonding σ, π or non-bonding n) to vacant antibonding orbitals (σ* or π*). Energy order of orbitals: σ < π < n < π* < σ*.
Types of transitions:
(i) σ → σ*: requires highest energy, λ < 150 nm (vacuum UV); shown by saturated hydrocarbons, e.g. methane (122 nm), ethane (135 nm).
(ii) n → σ*: saturated compounds with lone pairs (alcohols, amines, halides, ethers); 150–250 nm, e.g. water 167 nm, CH3Cl 173 nm.
(iii) π → π*: alkenes, alkynes, carbonyls, aromatics; 170–250 nm for isolated, longer for conjugated systems; high intensity (ε = 103–104).
(iv) n → π*: lowest energy; compounds with both lone pair and π bond (C=O, N=O, C=S); 250–350 nm; weak and forbidden (ε = 10–100), e.g. acetone ≈ 280 nm.

Shifts: Bathochromic (red) shift – λmax moves to longer wavelength (by auxochrome, conjugation or solvent); hypsochromic (blue) shift – to shorter wavelength; hyperchromic effect – increase in absorption intensity (ε); hypochromic effect – decrease in intensity.

Oxygen molecule (O2): has σ and π bonds and lone pairs, so possible transitions are σ → σ*, π → π* and n → π* (n → σ*); in the ground state the unpaired electrons in π* orbitals also allow π* → σ* transitions.

Benzene: only σ and π electrons, no lone pairs, so σ → σ* (very high energy, vacuum UV) and π → π* transitions occur. The π → π* gives three bands: 184 nm (E1, ε ≈ 47000), 204 nm (E2, ε ≈ 7000) and the weak, fine-structured 254 nm (B-band, ε ≈ 200, symmetry forbidden).
formulas: σ → σ* > n → σ* > π → π* > n → π* (energy order)

rubric.point: Conjugation in butadiene lowers the HOMO–LUMO gap (explanation with MO)
Ethane only σ → σ* (≈135 nm) vs butadiene π → π* (217 nm)
Statement of Beer-Lambert law with equation A = εcl
Any two applications of UV-Vis

answer: Ethane has only σ electrons, so its only transition is σ → σ*, which needs very high energy (λmax ≈ 135 nm). 1,3-Butadiene has two conjugated C=C bonds; the four p orbitals combine to give four π molecular orbitals (ψ1–ψ4). The interaction of the two π systems raises the HOMO (ψ2) and lowers the LUMO (ψ3) relative to isolated ethene, so the HOMO–LUMO gap decreases.

Because ΔE = hc/λ, a smaller ΔE means longer wavelength: butadiene absorbs by π → π* at λ<sub>max</sub> = 217 nm (ethene 165 nm), far above ethane's 135 nm. More conjugation gives a further red shift.

Beer-Lambert law: the absorbance of a solution is directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing species and to the path length of the cell: A = log(I0/I) = εcl, where ε is the molar absorptivity (L mol−1 cm−1), c the concentration (mol L−1), l the path length (cm).

Applications: quantitative estimation of unknown concentrations; detection of conjugation/functional groups (chromophores); study of reaction kinetics and equilibria; determination of purity of compounds; finding dissociation constants of acids/indicators; analysis of metal complexes (colorimetry).

rubric.point: Number of vibrational modes: 3N − 5 for linear, 3N − 6 for non-linear
Modes of CO<sub>2</sub>/CS<sub>2</sub> (linear): symmetric stretch, asymmetric stretch, doubly degenerate bend, with IR activity
Modes of H<sub>2</sub>O (bent): three modes, all IR-active
Condition for IR activity: change in dipole moment
IR-inactive molecules among list (H<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>) and CH<sub>4</sub> note, with reasons

answer: Number of fundamental vibrations: non-linear molecule 3N − 6; linear molecule 3N − 5. For AB2 (N = 3) this is 3 modes for bent H2O and 4 modes for linear CO2 and CS2.

Water (bent, C2v) – 3 modes: (i) symmetric stretch ν1 ≈ 3652 cm−1; (ii) bending (scissoring) ν2 ≈ 1595 cm−1; (iii) asymmetric stretch ν3 ≈ 3756 cm−1. All three change the dipole moment, so all are IR-active.

CO2 and CS2 (linear, O=C=O) – 4 modes: (i) symmetric stretch ν1 (both C=O lengthen together; CO2 1388 cm−1): dipole stays zero, so IR-inactive (Raman-active); (ii) asymmetric stretch ν3 (2349 cm−1 for CO2): one bond shortens while the other lengthens, dipole changes, IR-active; (iii) and (iv) bending ν2 (667 cm−1), two mutually perpendicular degenerate modes (in the plane and out of the plane), dipole changes, IR-active (counted as one absorption band).

Condition for IR activity: a vibration is IR-active only if it produces a net change in the dipole moment of the molecule (Δμ ≠ 0 during vibration); in addition the radiation frequency must match the vibrational frequency (hν = ΔE, with the vibrational selection rule Δv = ±1 for the harmonic oscillator).

Which molecules do not absorb IR: homonuclear diatomics H2 and N2 have no permanent dipole and none develops on stretching, so they are IR-inactive. CO (heteronuclear, dipole changes on stretching) is IR-active (≈ 2143 cm−1). CO2 absorbs through its asymmetric stretch and bend. CH4 (tetrahedral, zero dipole) absorbs through its asymmetric stretch (3019 cm−1) and bend (1306 cm−1) as these produce a changing dipole; only its totally symmetric stretch is IR-inactive. Thus the only molecules that show no IR absorption at all are H2 and N2.

rubric.point: Fingerprint region 400–1400 cm<sup>−1</sup> consists of complex absorption from C–C, C–O, C–N stretches and bending vibrations
Pattern is unique to each molecule (like a human fingerprint); even close homologues differ
Use: identification by matching with a reference spectrum

answer: The region from about 400 to 1400 cm<sup>−1</sup> contains a very large number of overlapping absorptions: single-bond stretches (C–C, C–O, C–N, C–X) and many skeletal bending, rocking, twisting and wagging vibrations. These have similar energies and also couple with each other, so the bands are numerous and complex.

The exact pattern depends on the whole molecular skeleton: even a small change in structure (e.g. one additional CH<sub>2</sub> or a different position of a substituent) changes this region considerably. Hence no two different compounds, except enantiomers, give the same pattern here, just as no two persons have the same fingerprint.

Therefore this region is called the fingerprint region. It is not used to identify individual functional groups (done in 1400–4000 cm−1), but an unknown compound is confirmed by an exact match of its fingerprint region with the spectrum of an authentic sample.

rubric.point: Definition: [4+2] cycloaddition of a conjugated diene with a dienophile giving cyclohexene
Example reaction (1,3-butadiene + ethene / maleic anhydride) with equation
Concerted, single-step, cyclic transition state; 4π + 2π electrons; suprafacial
Requirements: s-cis diene, electron-poor dienophile, stereospecific (syn addition; endo rule)
Diagram / orbital interaction (HOMO–LUMO)

answer: Diels-Alder reaction is a thermal [4 + 2] cycloaddition between a conjugated diene (4π electrons) and an alkene or alkyne called the dienophile (2π electrons) to give a six-membered ring (cyclohexene derivative), forming two new σ bonds at the expense of two π bonds.

Example: 1,3-butadiene + maleic anhydride → cis-tetrahydrophthalic anhydride (cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylic anhydride) on heating in benzene/xylene. Simple example: CH2=CH–CH=CH2 + CH2=CH–CHO → cyclohex-3-enecarbaldehyde.

Mechanism: it is a concerted, pericyclic reaction with no intermediate. The diene (in s-cis conformation) and dienophile approach in parallel planes. Bond formation between the diene termini C-1 and C-4 and the two dienophile carbons occurs simultaneously through a six-membered cyclic aromatic-like transition state containing 6 delocalised π electrons (thermally allowed by the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, [π4s + π2s]).
The diene double bonds shift: the new C=C forms between C-2 and C-3 of the diene, giving the cyclohexene ring.

Orbital picture: normal electron-demand: HOMO of the diene overlaps in phase with the LUMO of the dienophile, which is why electron-withdrawing groups (–CHO, –COOR, –CN, anhydride) on the dienophile and electron-donating groups on the diene increase the rate.

Stereochemistry: stereospecific syn addition, so the relative configuration of substituents on the dienophile is retained (cis-dienophile gives cis-product, trans gives trans). With cyclic dienes such as cyclopentadiene the endo product is favoured (Alder endo rule, secondary orbital overlap).
Importance: a key method for synthesis of six-membered rings and polycyclic compounds, with 100 % atom economy.

rubric.point: Addition vs substitution: definitions with examples
Tabular differences (bond change, unsaturation, product)
Mechanism of substitution (S<sub>N</sub>1/S<sub>N</sub>2 or electrophilic aromatic substitution)
(i) Electrophilic addition: mechanism with example (HBr + ethene / Markovnikov)
(ii) Nucleophilic addition: mechanism with example (HCN + carbonyl)

answer: Addition reaction: two molecules combine to give a single product; a π bond is broken and two new σ bonds form, so unsaturation decreases. Example: CH2=CH2 + Br2 → BrCH2CH2Br. Typical of alkenes, alkynes, aldehydes and ketones.

Substitution reaction: an atom or group in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group; the unsaturation is unchanged and two products are formed. Example: CH3Cl + OH− → CH3OH + Cl−; C6H6 + HNO3 → C6H5NO2 + H2O. Typical of alkanes, alkyl halides and arenes.

Differences: addition – σ + π bond change, one product, occurs in unsaturated compounds, mechanism electrophilic/nucleophilic/free radical; substitution – only σ bonds change, two products, occurs in saturated compounds and aromatics (SN1, SN2, SEAr).

Mechanism of substitution (SN2): Nu− attacks the carbon from the backside of the leaving group, giving a [Nu···C···X] transition state in one step with inversion of configuration; SN1 goes through a carbocation. In arenes the electrophile forms an arenium ion (σ-complex) that loses H+ to restore aromaticity.

(i) Electrophilic addition (alkenes): addition of HBr to propene. Step 1: the π electrons attack H+ of HBr (slow) forming the more stable secondary carbocation CH3–C+H–CH3 + Br−. Step 2: Br− attacks the carbocation (fast) giving 2-bromopropane. This follows Markovnikov's rule (H adds to the carbon having more hydrogens).

(ii) Nucleophilic addition (carbonyl compounds): addition of HCN to acetaldehyde. Step 1: CN− (nucleophile) attacks the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon (slow), the C=O π electrons move to oxygen giving an alkoxide ion CH3CH(CN)O−. Step 2: the alkoxide takes H+ from HCN/H2O to give the cyanohydrin CH3CH(OH)CN. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones (less steric hindrance and positive charge).

rubric.point: Balanced equation: salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin + acetic acid
Conditions: few drops conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> catalyst, warm at 50–60 °C ~15 min
Mechanism: nucleophilic acyl substitution (protonation of anhydride, attack by phenolic OH, tetrahedral intermediate, loss of acetic acid)
Work-up: cooling, addition of water, crystallisation / recrystallisation from ethanol-water; m.p. 135–136 °C

answer: Reaction (acetylation of salicylic acid): 2-HO–C6H4–COOH (salicylic acid) + (CH3CO)2O (acetic anhydride) → 2-CH3COO–C6H4–COOH (acetylsalicylic acid, aspirin) + CH3COOH.

Conditions: salicylic acid is warmed with excess acetic anhydride in the presence of a few drops of conc. H2SO4 (or H3PO4) as acid catalyst at about 50–60 °C for 15–20 minutes. The mixture is cooled and water is added to decompose excess anhydride and precipitate the product; the crude aspirin is filtered and recrystallised from ethanol–water (m.p. 135–136 °C).
Mechanism (nucleophilic acyl substitution, addition–elimination):
Step 1: the acid protonates a carbonyl oxygen of acetic anhydride, making its carbonyl carbon much more electrophilic.
Step 2: the lone pair on the phenolic –OH oxygen of salicylic acid attacks this carbon (nucleophilic addition), giving a tetrahedral intermediate.
Step 3: proton transfer within the intermediate converts the acetate group into a good leaving group (acetic acid).
Step 4: the C=O reforms, expelling CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (elimination), and loss of H<sup>+</sup> from the oxonium oxygen gives aspirin and regenerates the catalyst.
Aspirin (analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, antiplatelet) is thus obtained in about 80–90 % yield.

rubric.point: Degree of unsaturation = 0, saturated alkyl bromide
Total H count 6 + 1 + 2 = 9 matches C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br
δ 1.04 (6H, d): two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub> on a CH
δ 1.95 (1H, m): CH coupled to 6 + 2 = 8 neighbouring H
δ 3.33 (2H, d): CH<sub>2</sub>Br attached to one CH, deshielded by Br

answer: Formula C4H9Br: degree of unsaturation = (2×4 + 2 − 9 − 1)/2 = 0, so the compound is a saturated alkyl bromide. The integration 6H + 1H + 2H = 9H agrees with all nine hydrogens.

δ 1.04 (6H, doublet): six equivalent protons = two equivalent CH3 groups, upfield (typical alkyl). A doublet (n + 1 = 2) means each CH3 has one neighbouring H: they are attached to a CH, i.e. (CH3)2CH–.
δ 1.95 (1H, multiplet): the methine proton CH, coupled with 6 (from two CH3) + 2 (from CH2) = 8 neighbours, giving a nonet seen as a multiplet.
δ 3.33 (2H, doublet): two protons strongly deshielded (δ 3–4) by the electronegative bromine: –CH2Br. A doublet means one neighbouring H, i.e. attached to the CH.
Structure: (CH3)2CH–CH2–Br, isobutyl bromide (1-bromo-2-methylpropane).

Other isomers rejected: n-butyl bromide would show a triplet (3H) and a CH2Br triplet; sec-butyl bromide (CH3CH2CHBrCH3) has a 3H triplet, 3H doublet, and 1H sextet; tert-butyl bromide shows one 9H singlet. Only isobutyl bromide fits 6H d, 1H m, 2H d.
